| `--search` | Matches a model's id, name or description. |
| `--limit` | Page size, 1–100. |
| `--after` | The `next_cursor` of the previous page. |

Models come back in the order `generate` and `generate_image` pick their default from: the platform's own first, then cheapest-first where a price is published. A video defaults to the first of the platform's video defaults the catalogue publishes — the standard video model, `black-forest-labs/flux-3-max`, `minimax/hailuo-3`, `bytedance/seedance-2.5`, then `alibaba/wan-3.0/text-to-video`; if the catalogue publishes none of them, you are asked to name one.

No price is on the reply. A generation is billed [what it cost](/docs/platform/pricing#media-generation--per-finished-job-media-component) once it finishes — nothing is held or checked beforehand, from the CLI, the API or a session; the debit lands once, when the render does. Training a [character](/docs/cli/character) is the exception: the balance must cover it first.

`--kind stt`, `--kind tts` and `--kind s2s` list the [audio models](/docs/api/audio#the-catalogues) the same way: the managed alias for that direction first, then pinned models cheapest-first where a price is published.

## stock

```bash theme={"system"}
naive media stock "office workspace" --count 3 --orientation landscape
```

```json theme={"system"}
{
  "data": [
    {
      "object": "stock_photo",
      "id": "2014422",
      "width": 3024,
      "height": 2016,
      "url": "https://images.example/2014422.jpeg?w=940",
      "preview_url": "https://images.example/2014422.jpeg?w=280",
      "alt": "Modern office workspace with laptop",
      "photographer": "Joey Farina",
      "attribution_url": "https://photos.example/photo/2014422/",
      "dominant_color": "#978E82",
      "file_name": "stock-2014422.jpeg"
    }
  ]
}
```

| Flag | Description |
| - | - |
| `--count` | How many photos, 1–30. Default 10. No cursor: `--count` is the whole page. |
| `--orientation` | `landscape`, `portrait` or `square`. |
| `--color` | A dominant colour — a name such as `brown`, or a hex value such as `#978E82`. |
| `--size` | Which size `url` points at: `small`, `medium` or `large`. Default `large`. Picks the rendition only — it does not narrow the results. |

Show `photographer`, linked to `attribution_url`, wherever you use the photo — that credit is what the licence asks for. To keep the bytes as a `fil_`, import `url` through [`naive file import`](/docs/cli/files) with the credit as `--description` and `file_name` as `--name`; through the API, pass `file_name` as the import's `name` so the stored file carries no library branding. A deploy with no stock photo library configured answers `feature_not_configured`.

## clip

```bash theme={"system"}
naive media clip https://cdn.example.com/keynote.mp4 --captions bold --language en --max-seconds 45
```

```json theme={"system"}
{
  "id": "med_01H9HH...",
  "object": "media_job",
  "kind": "clip",
  "status": "queued",
  "model": null,
  "input": { "video_url": "https://cdn.example.com/keynote.mp4", "aspect_ratio": "9:16", "remove_silence": false, "caption_preset": "bold", "language": "en", "min_seconds": 15, "max_seconds": 45, "title": null },
  "result": null,
  "error": null,
  "cost_micro_usd": null,
  "session_id": null,
  "created_at": "2026-09-06T18:00:00.000Z",
  "completed_at": null
}
```

| Flag | Description |
| - | - |
| `--aspect` | `9:16` (default, reframed to the speaker) or `16:9`. |
| `--captions` | `none` (default), `clean`, `bold` or `karaoke`. |
| `--language` | BCP-47 hint for transcription, e.g. `de`. Omit to detect. |
| `--min-seconds` | Shortest clip to keep, 5–180 (default 15). |
| `--max-seconds` | Longest clip to keep, 5–180 (default 60). |
| `--remove-silence` | Tighten pauses inside each clip. |
| `--title` | A title for clips the scorer does not name itself. |

The URL must be public `http(s)`; a private or loopback host is refused. The job is billed [what it actually cost](/docs/platform/pricing#media-generation--per-finished-job-media-component) once it finishes, and a submit is refused when the organization's balance is empty.

## clip show

```bash theme={"system"}
naive media clip show med_01H9HH...
```

The same object, moved on. Once `status` is `completed`, `result.clips` lists each clip's `file_id`, `title`, `start_seconds`, `end_seconds`, `duration_seconds` and `virality` scores (0–100), and `cost_micro_usd` is settled. Fetch a clip's bytes with [`naive file`](/docs/cli/files).

```bash theme={"system"}
naive media clip show med_01H9HH... | jq -r '.result.clips[] | "\(.virality.total)\t\(.title)\t\(.file_id)"'
```

## clips

```bash theme={"system"}
naive media clips --status completed --limit 20
```

| Flag | Description |
| - | - |
| `--status` | `queued`, `processing`, `completed` or `failed`. |
| `--limit` | Page size, 1–100. |
| `--after` | The `next_cursor` of the previous page. |

Only jobs submitted with `naive media clip` or the API are listed; what an agent's `clip_video` tool cuts inside a session lands in that session as files.

## skills

```bash theme={"system"}
naive media skills build https://www.instagram.com/reel/C1abc/ https://www.instagram.com/reel/C2def/ --name "Slow feast" --wait
naive media skills revise ctp_01H9HH... --feedback "Slower cuts, warmer color grade" --wait
naive media skills get ctp_01H9HH...
naive media skills list --state ready
```

`build` takes one to three public reel links and queues a [skill build](/docs/api/media-skills); every round that comes back `ready` is saved as the next version of one org skill. `revise` runs the next round from your feedback. `get` reads a build and moves it forward; `list` does not. With `--wait`, the command follows the newest round until it is `ready` and prints the build with `skill_ref` (`slug@version`), or exits 1 when the round fails.

| Flag | Description |
| - | - |
| `--name` | `build`: a name for the skill (up to 80 characters). |
| `--description` | `build`: what the skill is for (up to 2000 characters). |
| `--feedback` | `revise`: what to change (required). |
| `--wait` | `build`, `revise`: poll until the round is `ready` or `failed`. |
| `--state` | `list`: `setup`, `building` or `ready`. |
| `--limit` | `list`: page size, 1–100. |
| `--after` | `list`: the `next_cursor` of the previous page. |

## transcribe

```bash theme={"system"}
naive media transcribe ./earnings-call.mp3 --language en
naive media transcribe https://cdn.example.com/earnings-call.mp3
naive media transcribe fil_01j9x3c2g8h4k5m6n7p8q9r0s1
```

A local path is uploaded first as a published [file](/docs/cli/files), then transcribed; an `http(s)` URL or a `fil_` id is sent as-is. Prints the [transcription job](/docs/api/audio#the-transcription-job) — usually already `completed` with `result.text` and `result.segments`; a long recording the provider queues prints `processing`, to be re-read with `naive media transcription`.

| Flag | Description |
| - | - |
| `--model` | A model from `naive media models --kind stt`. Omitted, the managed `stt/auto` alias. |
| `--language` | ISO 639-1 hint, e.g. `en`. Omitted, the model detects it. |
| `--no-timestamps` | Skip per-segment timestamps. |

## transcription

```bash theme={"system"}
naive media transcription med_01j9x3c2g8h4k5m6n7p8q9r0s1
```

The same job, by id.

## speak

```bash theme={"system"}
naive media speak "Your order has shipped and arrives Thursday." --voice alloy --format wav
```

Prints the speech generation: `model`, `cost_micro_usd`, and the stored `file`. The bytes are one [`naive file download`](/docs/cli/files) away:

```bash theme={"system"}
naive media speak "Hello." | jq -r .file.id | xargs naive file download > hello.wav
```

| Flag | Description |
| - | - |
| `--model` | A model from `naive media models --kind tts`. Omitted, [the default speech model](/docs/api/audio#speak). |
| `--voice` | One of the model's voices. Omitted, the model's default. |
| `--format` | `mp3` (default), `wav` or `ogg` — a preference: the catalogue's models answer WAV whatever is asked. |
| `--speed` | 0.5–2. Omitted, the model's own pace. |

## edit

```bash theme={"system"}
naive media edit "the same people, on a rooftop at dusk" --video fil_01J... --mode scene
naive media edit "swap the person for the one in the photo" --video fil_01J... --reference fil_01K... --mode person_swap --wait
```

`POST /v1/media/edits`. `--video` is a library video or a public URL. `--reference` repeats, up to four pictures. `--mode` is `scene`, `outfit_or_object`, `person_swap` or `recast`. `--wait` polls `GET /v1/media/edits/{id}` until the edit finishes.

## sound-effect

```bash theme={"system"}
naive media sound-effect "a heavy wooden door slamming shut, echoing" --seconds 3
```

Generates a short clip from a description — ambience, foley, a sting — and prints the sound generation: the stored `file`, its `duration_seconds` and `cost_micro_usd`. Add `--loop` for seamless ambience. The bytes are one [`naive file download`](/docs/cli/files) away:

```bash theme={"system"}
naive media sound-effect "rain on a tin roof" | jq -r .file.id | xargs naive file download > rain.mp3
```

| Flag | Description |
| - | - |
| `--seconds` | Clip length in seconds, 0.5–30; decimals allowed. Omitted, the generator fits the length to the prompt. |
| `--loop` | Make the clip loop seamlessly — for ambience and backgrounds. |

## music

```bash theme={"system"}
naive media music "an upbeat synthwave track with driving bass and bright arpeggios" --seconds 30
```

Generates an original song from a description — any genre, mood or instrumentation — and prints the music generation: the stored `file`, its `duration_seconds` and `cost_micro_usd`. Add `--instrumental` for a track with no vocals. The bytes are one [`naive file download`](/docs/cli/files) away:

```bash theme={"system"}
naive media music "a mellow lo-fi beat to study to" | jq -r .file.id | xargs naive file download > beat.mp3
```

| Flag | Description |
| - | - |
| `--seconds` | Song length in seconds, 3–300; decimals allowed. Omitted, 30. |
| `--instrumental` | Force an instrumental track with no vocals. |

## converse

```bash theme={"system"}
naive media converse ./question.wav --format wav
naive media converse https://cdn.example.com/question.wav
naive media converse fil_01j9x3f0a1b2c3d4e5f6g7h8j9 --voice sage
```

One spoken turn in, the spoken reply out. A local path is uploaded and a public URL is [imported](/docs/cli/files) into the library first — the [route](/docs/api/audio#converse) takes a stored `fil_` only; a `fil_` id is sent as-is. Prints the same speech generation `speak` does:

```bash theme={"system"}
naive media converse ./question.wav | jq -r .file.id | xargs naive file download > reply.wav
```

| Flag | Description |
| - | - |
| `--model` | A model from `naive media models --kind s2s`. Omitted, the managed `s2s/auto` alias. |
| `--voice` | One of the model's voices. Omitted, the model's default. |
| `--format` | `mp3` (default), `wav` or `ogg` — a preference: the catalogue's models reply in WAV whatever is asked. |

## Pinning a model on an agent

```bash theme={"system"}
naive media models --kind video --search seedance --limit 1 | jq -r '.data[0].id'
```

# naive mobile
Source: https://usenaive.ai/docs/cli/mobile

Provision and drive cloud Android phones and iPhones.

Manage [mobile devices](/docs/computer/mobile) — cloud phones you look at, tap, type into and destroy. The third member of the computer suite beside [`naive computer`](/docs/cli/computer).

## Commands

| Command | Description |
| - | - |
| `naive mobile create` | Create a device. |
| `naive mobile list` | List devices (terminated ones excluded). |
| `naive mobile show <id>` | Show a device, reconciled with the provider. |
| `naive mobile update <id>` | Rename a device. |
| `naive mobile act <id>` | Run one action: tap, type, press a key, scroll, open a URL, install an app, look. |
| `naive mobile install <id> <app>` | Install an app from the platform's app catalogue on the running phone. |
| `naive mobile screenshot <id>` | Take a screenshot; `--out` writes the JPEG. |
| `naive mobile live-view <id>` | Print the device's dashboard link, where its live stream plays. |
| `naive mobile delete <id>` | End the device. |

`naive mobile list --session-id ses_…` lists only the phone that agent session opened.

## create

```bash theme={"system"}
naive mobile create --name pixel --os-version 15 --idle-timeout-minutes 15
naive mobile create --name iphone --platform ios --apps com.burbn.instagram
```

| Flag | Description |
| - | - |
| `--name` | Human-readable name (default `device`). |
| `--platform` | `android` (the default) or `ios`. |
| `--os-version` | Android only: `13`, `14` or `15` (default `15`). An iPhone has no version to choose; passing one with `--platform ios` is `validation_failed` (400). |
| `--model` | `phone` (the default, and today the only value). |
| `--jurisdiction` | `us`, `eu` or `as` (default `us`): the phone runs in the US, Germany or Singapore, and its traffic exits through a residential IP in that country, with GPS, timezone, locale and carrier to match. |
| `--idle-timeout-minutes` | Inactivity after which the device ends, 1–180 (default `10`). |
| `--max-duration-minutes` | Hard ceiling on its life, 1–1440 (default `120`). |
| `--apps` | Comma-separated app ids, installed from the platform's app catalogue when the device starts: package names on Android (`com.spotify.music`), App Store bundle ids on iOS (`com.burbn.instagram`). |

The command waits up to about 45 seconds for the phone and answers with whatever is true then, usually `"status": "creating"`: an Android phone is usually ready in under a minute (a few with apps at create) and an iPhone in up to about three, and `naive mobile show` follows it. There is no pause: the two timers are how idle cost is controlled.

There is no limit on how many phones you run, only on the balance: a create needs 10 minutes for every live phone and the new one at their rates (`$0.50` for one Android phone, `$0.80` for one iPhone), plus what the live ones have run, or it fails with `insufficient_credits` (402). When the platform's phones are all in use it fails with `rate_limited` (429); try again shortly.

## act

One verb over the whole action surface. `--type` picks the action; the other flags belong to it.

```bash theme={"system"}
naive mobile act mob_01H8YZ... --type tap --x 360 --y 1100
naive mobile act mob_01H8YZ... --type tap --text "Sign in"
naive mobile act mob_01H8YZ... --type type --text "hello"
naive mobile act mob_01H8YZ... --type press_key --key KEYCODE_BACK
naive mobile act mob_01H8YZ... --type scroll --direction down --amount 400
naive mobile act mob_01H8YZ... --type open_url --url https://example.com
naive mobile act mob_01H8YZ... --type launch_app --package com.android.settings
naive mobile act mob_01H8YZ... --type element_tree
naive mobile act mob_01H8YZ... --type install_app --app com.spotify.music
```

| Flag | Used by |
| - | - |
| `--type` | Required: `screenshot`, `element_tree`, `tap`, `type`, `press_key`, `scroll`, `open_url`, `launch_app`, `install_app`. |
| `--x`, `--y` | `tap` by coordinates; screenshot pixels map 1:1. |
| `--text` | `tap` by visible text, or the text for `type`. |
| `--resource-id`, `--content-desc` | `tap` by element id or accessibility label. |
| `--key` | `press_key`: `HOME`, `BACK`, `RECENTS`, `NOTIFICATIONS`, `ENTER`, `DEL`, `TAB`, `ESCAPE`, `SPACE`, arrows (`DPAD_*`), volume, `POWER`, or a numeric key code; case-insensitive, a `KEYCODE_` prefix is accepted. These are Android's keys: an iPhone has no `BACK` or `RECENTS`, so navigate it with taps and `HOME`. |
| `--direction`, `--amount` | `scroll`: `up`, `down`, `left`, `right`; `--amount` is optional, in screenshot pixels (default: 40% of the screen). |
| `--url` | `open_url`. |
| `--package` | `launch_app`: an installed app's package name, e.g. `com.android.settings`. |
| `--app` | `install_app`: a package name (Android) or App Store bundle id (iOS). |

A `tap` with neither coordinates nor a selector is a usage error, not a request.

## install

```bash theme={"system"}
naive mobile install mob_01H8YZ... com.spotify.music
```

The same as `act --type install_app --app …`: installs the app from the platform's app catalogue onto the running phone, with no upload and no store account. The catalogue carries many but not all store apps and cannot be listed; an app it lacks fails in a second or two (`400`, `param: app`), so this is also how to check one before naming it in `--apps`. It waits up to about a minute and prints `{ "object": "mobile_action_result", "type": "install_app", "output": { "app": "com.spotify.music", "status": "installed", "error": null }, "image": null }`. `status` is `installed`, `failed` (with `error`), or `installing` when a large app is still going: run the same command again to check on it.

## screenshot

```bash theme={"system"}
naive mobile screenshot mob_01H8YZ... --out shot.jpg
```

Without `--out` the JSON result is printed, the image bytes base64-encoded in `image.data`. With it, the JPEG bytes are written to the path and the command prints `{ "path": "shot.jpg", "content_type": "image/jpeg" }`.

## live-view

```bash theme={"system"}
naive mobile live-view mob_01H8YZ...
```

Prints `{ "object": "mobile_live_view", "url": "https://…/mobile/mob_…", "expires_at": null }`. `url` is the device's dashboard page, where the stream plays. The CLI never prints the `stream` half of the answer: it is a bearer credential (anyone holding it drives the device until it ends), and a terminal's output ends up in scrollback and CI logs. Each mint is recorded in the audit log without the credential.

## show, update, delete

```bash theme={"system"}
naive mobile show mob_01H8YZ...
naive mobile update mob_01H8YZ... --name "qa phone"
naive mobile delete mob_01H8YZ...
```

`show` asks the provider and reports the truth — a device ended by its idle timer comes back `terminated` with `termination_reason: "idle_timeout"`. `list` reads stored rows only and can lag until a `show`.


# naive models
Source: https://usenaive.ai/docs/cli/models

List the models an agent can be created against.

`naive models list` is how you learn a legal `--model` for [`naive agent create`](/docs/cli/agents#create), which requires one.

There is **no fixed list**. The catalogue is read live from the network, so a model published today is runnable today — and hundreds are catalogued, which is why the listing pages and searches.

## Commands

| Command | Description |
| - | - |
| `naive models list` | List available models, optionally narrowed to one completion window. |
| `naive models get <id>` | One model by id, for the id you already hold. |

## list

```bash theme={"system"}
naive models list --search glm --limit 2
```

```json theme={"system"}
{
  "data": [
    {
      "object": "model",
      "id": "zai-org/GLM-5.2-FP8",
      "context_window": 1048576,
      "max_output_tokens": 32768,
      "supported_windows": ["immediate", "priority", "loose"],
      "efforts": ["low", "medium", "high"]
    },
    {
      "object": "model",
      "id": "moonshotai/Kimi-K2.6",
      "context_window": 262144,
      "max_output_tokens": 16384,
      "supported_windows": ["immediate", "priority", "loose"],
      "efforts": ["low", "medium", "high"]
    }
  ],
  "has_more": true,
  "next_cursor": "2"
}
```

| Flag | Description |
| - | - |
| `--window` | Narrow to models servable in one [completion window](/docs/concepts/model-router): `immediate` \| `priority` \| `loose`. |
| `--search` | Matches a model's id and name. |
| `--limit` | Page size, 1–100. Defaults to 20. |
| `--after` | The `next_cursor` of the previous page. |

`context_window` is in tokens. `max_output_tokens` is the longest reply that model may produce, and what the pre-flight quote is bounded by. `supported_windows` is the authoritative list of windows that model can actually be served in — an `agent create` naming a window outside it is rejected.

No price is on the reply. What an agent spends is bounded by its own budget, and read back with [`naive agent spend`](/docs/cli/agents#spend).

One id in the listing is not a specific model: `vetta/auto` picks one per request. It serves `immediate` only — see [Naive Managed Agents Auto](/docs/concepts/model-router#naive-managed-agents-auto).

## get

```bash theme={"system"}
naive models get zai-org/GLM-5.2-FP8
```

```json theme={"system"}
{
  "object": "model",
  "id": "zai-org/GLM-5.2-FP8",
  "context_window": 1048576,
  "max_output_tokens": 32768,
  "supported_windows": ["immediate", "priority", "loose"],
  "efforts": ["low", "medium", "high"]
}
```

An id this deploy does not serve is a `not_found` error, so this is also how you check a model id before you run an agent on it.

## Not every model serves every window

`immediate` is served by every catalogued model. `priority` and `loose` are served only by the
models the completion-window pool hosts, and `supported_windows` on each row is the authoritative
answer — it is derived from the rate card the router prices against, so a model listed for a window
can never be refused for it.

```bash theme={"system"}
naive models list --window loose
```

```json theme={"system"}
{
  "data": [
    {
      "object": "model",
      "id": "google/gemma-4-31B-it",
      "context_window": 131072,
      "max_output_tokens": 16384,
      "supported_windows": ["immediate", "priority", "loose"],
      "efforts": []
    }
  ],
  "has_more": true,
  "next_cursor": "1"
}
```

Naming a window a model does not serve is refused with `window_unavailable` (HTTP 400) before any
inference runs — never silently downgraded to a dearer window. So list first, then create.

## Picking a model in a script

```bash theme={"system"}
naive models list --window immediate --limit 1 | jq -r '.data[0].id'
```


# naive
Source: https://usenaive.ai/docs/cli/naive

Claim a cloned blueprint repo, apply its naive.config, scaffold a new one.

Installing the CLI package gives you the `naive` command. A cloned blueprint repository documents the
spellings below.

> [!NOTE]
>
> The blueprint × template table below is **bundled into the binary**, so `--template` only knows the
> templates the release you installed knew. A blueprint repo pins the CLI and gets the binary from its own
> `pnpm install`, so nothing global is required: `pnpm exec naive up`. To install it yourself,
> `npm i -g @usenaive-sdk/cli`.

## Commands

| Command | Description |
| - | - |
| `naive claim` | Bind the clone to your organization by storing a verified API key. |
| `naive up` | Reconcile `naive.config.*` against the platform, record the apply, and report what changed. |
| `naive init` | Scaffold a starter `naive.config.ts`. |
| `naive template` | Clone a published blueprint into a directory of its own. |
| `naive catalog` | List the published blueprint × template pairs and the versions they are published at. |
| `naive installs` | List what this organization has applied: project, blueprint, template, revision. |
| `naive installs context` | Print, or with `--set` edit, what the crew of the project in this directory knows about the business. |
| `naive installs remove` | Take a template out of the company: its crew is fired and its install goes. |

## claim

```bash theme={"system"}
naive claim --key sk_live_…
# or
export NAIVE_API_KEY=sk_live_…
naive claim
# or pipe it, so the key never appears in argv or the shell history
naive claim < key.txt
```

| Flag | Description |
| - | - |
| `--key` | The platform API key. Falls back to `NAIVE_API_KEY` (or `NAIVE_API_KEY`), then piped stdin. |

The key is verified with one authenticated read before anything is written; a refused key stores
nothing. On success the profile is saved owner-only (`0600`) and the output confirms the
organization and the key's 12-character display prefix — never the key itself.

The binding **is** the key: API keys are organization-scoped, so everything a later `naive up`
creates lands in that key's organization. The profile lives on this machine only — there is no
server-side record tying a repository or project name to an organization, so the same clone
claimed on another machine with another key deploys to another org. To move a project, claim
again with the other organization's key.

## up

```bash theme={"system"}
naive up --dry-run
naive up --dir ./blueprint
naive up --without analyst
naive up --only editor,site
```

| Flag | Description |
| - | - |
| `--dry-run` | Plan only: reads happen, writes do not, and the report says what apply would do. |
| `--dir` | Directory holding `naive.config.{ts,js,mjs,json}` (default: the current directory). |
| `--adopt` | Take over every app this run touches that another project owns, or that no project owns. |
| `--only` | Provision only these agents and apps, by declared name; comma-separated, repeatable. |
| `--without` | Provision everything except these agents and apps, by declared name; comma-separated, repeatable. |

The report names the `blueprint` and the `template` it applied, when the config declares them: a
crew provisioned into your organization is money, so which crew it was is not left to be inferred
from the agent list.

Loads the config, then reconciles each declared skill, identity, vault, app, agent and task by name —
in that order, so agents can reference the rest and cards can name their assignee. The report lists every resource as `created`,
`updated`, `unchanged`, `deleted` or `refused` (with the reason), and any refusal makes the exit
code non-zero. Re-running is always safe: every resource is keyed by its config name, and nothing
is deleted by omission — only a `removed` name, or a cron missing from an agent's `schedules`.

A live row the CLI cannot read — one written before a field's rules tightened, say — is listed
under `skipped` in the report and stepped over: it is neither reconciled nor deleted, and the rest
of the apply runs normally. A row in `skipped` is a row to fix or delete by hand.

### Config surface

| Key | Fields | Reconciled by |
| - | - | - |
| `name` | project name | — |
| `blueprint` | the machine this project runs | — (validated at define time) |
| `template` | which of that blueprint's templates provides the crew | — (validated at define time) |
| `title?`, `description?`, `platforms?` | what a person calls the template (≤ 80), one line on what it does (≤ 280), and the networks it publishes to | — (printed on the catalogue, never provisioned) |
| `questions[]` | `key`, `label`, `type`, `help?`, `optional?`, `options?`, `multiple?`, `other?`, `placeholder?` | — (asked before the apply, not reconciled by it) |
| `skills[]` | `slug`, `file` | slug; content hash decides `unchanged` vs `updated` |
| `identities[]` | `name`, `description?`, `legal?`, `wallet?`, `cards?` | name; `description` drift is patched |
| `identities[].legal[]` | `label`, `state`, `name_options`, `naics_code`, `description` | `label`; reported and never provisioned (a person starts a check or pays a formation) — see [Legal](/docs/identity/legal#infrastructure-as-code) |
| `identities[].wallet` | `network?`, `policy?: { per_tx_cap_micro_usd, daily_cap_micro_usd?, low_balance_micro_usd? }` | presence; `policy` drift is patched; never funded, frozen or swept — see [Wallet](/docs/identity/wallet#in-a-blueprint) |
| `identities[].cards[]` | `label`, `load_micro_usd` | `label`; issued (debiting credits) when no live card carries it; never cancelled or refunded — see [Cards](/docs/identity/cards#in-a-blueprint) |
| `vaults[]` | `name`, `identity?`, `credentials[]: { kind, key, host?, mcp_server_url?, value: { from_env } }` | name; credentials by presence |
| `apps[]` | `name`, `type`, `description?`, `deploy_dir?`, `env?`, `mcp?`, `migrations?`, `buckets?`, `required?` | name; `type` cannot change; `deploy_dir` by content hash; `mcp` patched on drift; `migrations` applied once each, by name; `buckets` created when missing, never deleted |
| `agents[]` | `name`, `model`, `budget`, `description?`, `system?`, `tools?`, `skills?`, `mcp_servers?`, `window?`, `multiagent?`, `handoffs?`, `output_schema?`, `structured_output_required?`, `metadata?`, `allowed_apps?`, `identity?`, `schedules?`, `intake?`, `role?`, `required?` | name; declared fields patched on drift |
| `agents[].schedules[]` | `cron`, `timezone?`, `input`, `budget_micro_usd`, `identity?`, `enabled?` | exact `cron`, as a complete set per agent |
| `agents[].intake` | `message`, `budget_micro_usd?` | sent once, on the apply that creates the agent |
| `tasks[]` | `key`, `title`, `body?`, `assignee?`, `blocked_by?` | `key`, as a card on the organization's board; `created` once, `unchanged` after |
| `removed` | `apps[]`, `agents[]`, `skills[]`, `identities[]`, `vaults[]` | name; tombstones |
| `kept` | `agents[]` | name; reported and never written (the switch rule below) |

Every cross-reference — `allowed_apps`, `identity`, a vault's `identity`, a roster's members — names a
resource declared in the same config, and a config that names one that is not declared (or declares a
name twice) is refused before anything is read. An agent's `system`, `skills`, `mcp_servers`,
`window`, `output_schema`, `structured_output_required` and `metadata` pass through to the platform
verbatim, exactly as `agents.create` takes them; `allowed_apps` names apps and is written as their ids
into the `apps` tool's config. `multiagent` is the agent's team setting as the platform spells it,
except that a roster names its members by their declared `name` (`{ type: "agent", name: "editor" }`
or just `"editor"`) instead of an id — `up` creates every agent first and then writes the roster with
the ids they were given. A roster may name an agent listed under `kept`, never one under `removed`.
`handoffs` is `true` (the platform's default: any agent of the organization), `false`, `"team"` (its own
`multiagent` roster, so the agent must declare one), or the declared `name`s this agent may
[send work to](/docs/capabilities/tools#handoffs) — checked against the same crew, so a name nobody declares,
the agent's own, or one written twice is refused before anything is read. A roster with
`handoffs: team` and `metadata: { role: group }` is a **channel** in the dashboard — a place whose
members are that roster. Nothing runs on it: a post with no mention asks every member, and an `@mention` asks just that member.
A field the config leaves out is never drift: the live value stays (an app's `mcp` is the one
exception — see below).

`questions` is the one key `up` does not reconcile, because it is not a resource: it is what a
person is asked **before** the crew is provisioned. They use the same shape an agent asks a question
with mid-run, so one form renders both, and the answers a person gives are recorded on the install
rather than written into the tree — the tree is identical for every organization running the same
template. Declaring them is what lets a published blueprint be set up before anything exists to
configure. A template declares at most four
([Templates](/docs/concepts/templates#four-questions-then-a-crew)); a hand-written config that names no
`template` is not capped.

`help` is the sentence shown under the label — where you say what a good answer looks like, so the
label can stay short. `optional: true` says the field may be left blank, and a blank one comes back
**absent**: the key is not in the answers at all, rather than present with an empty string, so an
unanswered question is simply not in the [project context](#installs-context) the crew reads. It is
for the question that would improve the work without gating it — a reference to imitate, say. Ask
that one mandatorily and you force an answer out of a person who has none, and an invented answer is
worse than an absent one, because the crew cannot tell them apart. A key you *do* send is checked
like any other: a blank string or an unlisted option is refused whether or not the field is
optional.

```ts theme={"system"}
export default defineProject({
  name: "my-project",
  skills: [{ slug: "clipping", file: "skills/clipping.md" }],
  identities: [{ name: "Ava", description: "Sales persona" }],
  agents: [
    {
      name: "clipper",
      model: "…",
      budget: { /* … */ },
      system: "Be terse.",
      skills: ["clipping"],
      mcp_servers: [{ name: "docs", url: "https://mcp.example/sse" }],
      identity: "Ava",
      tools: {
        default_config: { permission: "allow" },
        configs: {
          browser: {
            enabled: true,
            permission: "allow",
            config: { allowed_domains: ["example.com"], timeout_minutes: 30, context_name: "shop" },
          },
        },
      },
    },
  ],
});
```

An agent's `tools` is the platform's toolset verbatim, with one field checked at define time:
`tools.configs.browser.config` is the [browser's options](/docs/computer/browser#configuration-reference)
(`allowed_domains` optional — the open web by default, `timeout_minutes` 1–360, `context_name` to reopen a saved login, …).
A malformed one is refused by field (`agents.0.tools.configs.browser.config.allowed_domains`) rather
than applied — the runtime would otherwise open a browser that reaches nothing.

A skill's `file` (resolved against the config's directory) is pushed by slug; skills are
content-addressed, so an unchanged file is `unchanged` and a changed one mints a new version
(`updated`). An agent's `identity` names a declared identity, which `up` attaches after the agent
upsert; the grant is never revoked by `up`.

An agent's `tools` passes through as the same `configs` the API takes, so a blueprint can pin which
models `generate_image` / `generate_video` may render with — the first named is the default, and any
model must be in the live catalogue `naive media models --kind video` lists (see
[generation tools](/docs/capabilities/tools#generation-tools)):

```ts theme={"system"}
agents: [
  {
    name: "clipper",
    // …
    tools: {
      configs: {
        generate_video: { enabled: true, permission: "allow", config: { models: ["heygen/heygen-video-1"] } },
      },
    },
  },
],
```

An agent's `schedules` are its cron deployments, owned as a complete set:

```ts theme={"system"}
agents: [
  {
    name: "clipper",
    // …
    schedules: [
      { cron: "0 9 * * 1", timezone: "Europe/Berlin", input: "Post the weekly digest", budget_micro_usd: 500_000, identity: "Ava" },
      { cron: "0 * * * *", input: "Check the queue", budget_micro_usd: 50_000, enabled: false },
    ],
  },
],
```

Deployments have no name, so each schedule is matched to the agent's live deployments by its exact
`cron` string (which must be unique per agent): a match with other fields drifted is patched, a
missing cron is created, and any live deployment of that agent whose cron is not declared is
deleted. The set is bounded to agents declared in this config — an agent without `schedules` keeps
whatever it has, and other agents' deployments are never touched. Each outcome is a report line
named `<agent> @ <cron>` under `schedules`; a schedule `identity` names a declared identity.

> [!WARNING]
>
> The match is the cron **string**, not the schedule it denotes. `"0 8 * * 1"` and `"0 08 * * 1"` fire
> at the same minute and are two different keys, so re-spelling a declared cron is a delete plus a
> create, not a patch: the deployment gets a new `dep_` id and a fresh `next_run_at`, and anything the
> old row was holding — an `enabled: false`, say — is gone. `up` deliberately does not parse cron; a
> client that normalised the string would have to agree with the server's parser forever to stay
> idempotent, and the day they disagreed every apply would churn every schedule. Edit a cron and
> expect a new deployment.

### Taking part of the crew

A template's crew is provisioned whole unless you say otherwise. `--only` names the agents and apps
to take; `--without` names the ones to leave out; both take declared names and either kind. The
names left out come back in the report under **`deselected`**, apart from `skipped` (rows the CLI
could not read) and from any `refused` line (things it tried and could not do): a deselection is a
choice, and the report keeps choices apart from failures.

A deselected agent is not created, its `schedules` are not armed and its `intake` does not open — a
timer or a first session for an agent you declined is money spent on nobody's instruction. A
deselected agent that already exists is left running and reported `deselected`: narrowing the
selection is not `removed`, and retiring a live agent stays an explicit act.

A template may mark an agent or app `required` — the app every agent's tools reach through, say. A
selection that leaves one out is refused before a single route is called, and the message names
every missing one, in the same words the platform's own apply refuses it with:

```text theme={"system"}
selection leaves out required agent "editor", app "site"
```

A name the config does not declare is refused the same way. Selection is per apply and is not
remembered: a later `naive up` with neither flag provisions everything. See
[Templates](/docs/concepts/templates) for what a crew, its first day and its selection are.

### Tasks — the board the crew starts from

A project may declare `tasks`: the work its crew starts with, as cards on the organization's
shared board rather than as a briefing each agent reads alone.

```ts theme={"system"}
tasks: [
  { key: "draft", title: "Draft the first post", body: "Three candidates.", assignee: "clipper" },
  { key: "publish", title: "Publish the first post", assignee: "clipper", blocked_by: ["draft"] },
],
```

`key` is the task's stable name inside the project; `assignee` names an agent declared in the same
config (or one listed under `kept`); `blocked_by` names other tasks by key, and a key that is not
declared, an assignee that is not, a self-blocker, a cycle or a duplicate key is refused before
anything is read. Every card lives on the board of the organization's standing orchestrator — the
`CEO` the studio's Hire page creates — and `up` ensures that owner exists before it writes a card:
finds it by its `metadata.role`, creates it (as `CEO`, on a modest monthly budget) when the
organization has none, never renames one it finds, and seats this project's agents on its roster
so they can work the board. The owner is one line under `agents` in the report like any other
agent; the board is created if missing; each task is one line under `tasks`.

Cards are written blockers first, so `blocked_by` is always the ids of cards that already exist,
and each is keyed `<project>:<task.key>`. That key is what makes re-apply honest: a second
`naive up` finds every card already on the board and reports it `unchanged`, without a duplicate
and without touching what an agent has since moved to `doing` or `done`. Nothing in the apply
starts a session. A card with an `assignee` and no open blocker is picked up by the platform on
its next tick, which starts the assignee on that card — so a crew declared through `tasks` starts
working exactly once, and its first day is on the record where the whole crew can see it.
A card whose assignee this apply did not provision — deselected, or refused — is refused rather
than written, as are the cards behind it, so a board never names an agent that is not on it.
`--dry-run` plans the owner, the board and every card and writes none of them.

### The intake — the legacy first briefing

`intake` is the path `tasks` replaces: a private first session for one agent rather than a card
on the shared board. It keeps working exactly as it did, and a project may declare both — the
cards are seeded and the intakes opened, each reported under its own key — but a crew that starts
from a board should not also be briefed in private, so new templates declare `tasks` and leave
`intake` out.

An agent may declare an `intake`: the message it is sent **once, on the apply that creates it**.

```ts theme={"system"}
agents: [
  {
    name: "clipper",
    // …
    intake: { message: "Read the brief in the app and open your first three drafts.", budget_micro_usd: 250_000 },
  },
],
```

It is what turns a provisioned crew into a crew that has started working. It is not a schedule (a
schedule fires again and again) and not `system` (that is standing instruction, re-read every turn):
it is a session that is created and started with `message` as its first turn, reported under
`intake` as one line named after the agent whose `id` is the `ses_` that was opened.

Nothing marks an agent as briefed, because nothing needs to: an agent is created exactly once, so a
second `naive up` reports it `unchanged` and starts nothing. An agent that was merely patched is not
re-briefed. Delete the agent and apply again and it intakes again, which is the correct reading of
"this agent is new". `budget_micro_usd` is optional and caps that one session; leave it out and the
agent's own `budget` governs. Intakes are opened **last**, after every other write in the apply, so
an agent that delegates or reaches for an app finds the rest of the crew already there.

### Blueprints and templates

A **blueprint** is the machine: the screens, the `/api/*` routes, the store, the build and the
approval flow — or none of them, for a data-only blueprint whose crew works on the board. It is one
repository. A **template** is data inside that repository: the crew and its prompts, the tool
allow-lists and its schedules. A config names both:

```ts theme={"system"}
export default defineProject({
  name: "my-media",
  blueprint: "media",
  template: "clipping",
  templates: ALL_TEMPLATES, // every template this repo carries; the chosen one supplies `agents`
  apps: [/* … */],
});
```

| Blueprint | Templates | Default |
| - | - | - |
| `agency` | `blank`, `seo-geo` | `blank` |
| `media` | `faceless`, `longform`, `clipping` | none — you must choose |

`media` has no default on purpose: its three crews spend money in different ways — a long-form
piece renders a minute or more of video where a clip only cuts one — so defaulting any of them
would be a bill you did not choose. An unknown blueprint, an unknown template, or `media` with no
template at all is refused when the config is loaded — before anything is read or written.

The three `media` crews, by the id you pass to `--template` and the name the catalogue shows:

| `--template` | Name | What it makes |
| - | - | - |
| `faceless` | Faceless channel | Vertical shorts of 15–30 seconds, one render per piece. |
| `longform` | Long-form channel | Pieces of 60–180 seconds. Rendered as `ceil(seconds / 30)` segments of at most 30 seconds each — the measured cap of the model behind the render — then joined into one file by the producer before it publishes. |
| `clipping` | Clipping channel | Cuts 15–60 second vertical clips out of long videos you point it at. |

The ids are the wire: they are what a config, an install and `naive catalog --template` carry, and
they do not change when a name does. Each asks three setup questions. `faceless` and `longform` ask
the niche, a reference (optional) and how often to post; `clipping` asks the channels to cut from,
YouTube visibility (optional) and how often to post. None asks where to post: the crew posts to the
accounts you connect.

The chosen template's agents become the project's crew, and the config may declare agents of its
own alongside them. Because one repository carries every template its blueprint has, **switching
is an edit plus `naive up`** — never a re-clone, and never a new app: edit `template`, re-run, and
the machine, the app, its URL and its data stay exactly where they are.

Switching **widens and never narrows**. The new template's agents are created; an agent only the
previous template declared is reported and left alone — `defineProject` lists those names under
`kept`, and `up` reports each one that is live as `unchanged` with `not declared by template "…";
kept, never deleted`. Your own rows — clients, posts, connections, the app, its URL, its token —
are never touched by a switch. To retire an agent the old crew left behind, name it under
`removed` yourself, which is the only thing that ever deletes.

### App ownership

Every app records the project that created it, and `up` compares that stamp before it writes
anything. An app whose row names a different project — or no project, because it was made by hand
through the dashboard or the API — is **refused**, with the exit code non-zero and nothing written:

```
app "dashboard" is owned by project "seo-geo-agency"; this project is "faceless-media".
Rename the app in your config, or re-run `naive up --adopt` to transfer it.
```

App names are unique per organization, and an app is the one resource where taking a name over is
not recoverable: the deploy replaces a live site, an `env` write overwrites a secret value nothing
can read back, and a `removed` name tears down its hosting and its database. So a name collision
stops rather than converges. Fix it by renaming the app in your config, or, if the app really is
this project's, run `naive up --adopt` once: it takes every app the run touches, stamps each with
this project's `name`, and reports them `updated` with `adopted from project "…"` as the reason.
From then on ordinary `naive up` converges them and the flag is not needed again. `--adopt` covers
`removed` names too, since deleting another project's app is worse than overwriting it, and under
`--dry-run` it only says `will adopt …`.

An app's `env` is written as its secrets — a value is a literal or `{ from_env: "LOCAL_VAR" }`,
read from your shell at apply time so a secret never sits in the config file:

```ts theme={"system"}
apps: [
  {
    name: "dashboard",
    type: "fullstack",
    deploy_dir: "dist",
    env: { PUBLIC_URL: "https://dashboard.example", API_KEY: { from_env: "NAIVE_API_KEY" } },
  },
],
```

`{ from_env: "NAIVE_API_KEY" }` is the one exception: your own key never reaches the app. On the
apply that creates the app, `up` mints the app its own read-only key (listed among your API keys as
`app <name>`) and writes that instead. Minting needs an `admin` key in your shell; without one
the app is refused, naming `NAIVE_API_KEY`. A later apply leaves the minted key alone.

Secret values are write-only on the platform and never read back. Each write carries a hash of
the value, which the platform echoes on reads, so `up` can tell an unchanged secret from a changed
one without ever seeing a value: a secret whose live hash matches is skipped, and an app whose
secrets all match reports `unchanged`. Changing a `from_env` variable's value and re-running `up`
rewrites just that secret — **that is how rotation works for app secrets**. A secret set before
hashes existed (or by hand, through the dashboard or SDK) has no hash and is rewritten once. An
unset `from_env` variable refuses the app before any write, naming the variable only. Secrets that
exist on the app but are absent from `env` are listed in the report as `unmanaged secrets: …` and
left alone — nothing is deleted by omission. With `--dry-run` the report says `will set …` for
exactly the secrets an apply would write.

An app's `deploy_dir` ships as one file-map deployment carrying a hash of its contents. On the
next apply, `up` hashes the directory again and compares it with the app's newest deployment: equal
means nothing is uploaded and the app reports `unchanged` (unless `env` or `description` made it
`updated`); different, or a deployment made before hashes existed, deploys again. With `--dry-run`
the report says `will deploy <dir>` or `<dir> unchanged`.

A `fullstack` app's `mcp` is the path it serves an MCP endpoint on (`"/mcp"`): agents connected to
the app get its MCP tools automatically, and the platform mints a bearer token for that endpoint into
the app's `VETTA_MCP_TOKEN` secret, which the app should require. Declaring `mcp` on a
`frontend_only` app is refused at parse time. An unchanged path is `unchanged` (the token is never
rotated by a no-op apply); dropping `mcp` from the config clears the endpoint and forgets the token.
With `--dry-run` the report says `will set mcp <path>` or `will clear mcp`.

A `fullstack` app's `migrations` are SQL files applied to its [database](/docs/cli/database) after the
app is provisioned and deployed — paths under the config's directory, `*` allowed in the file name:
`["sql/*.sql"]`. Files match in name order within one entry and entries in declaration order, so
`0001_todos.sql`, `0002_index.sql` is the whole ordering story. Each file is a migration named by its
base name, applied **once**: a later apply re-sends the list and every already-applied one is a
no-op, so the report says `2 migration(s), 0 new` and the app is `unchanged` unless something was
new. Changing an applied file's contents under the same name is refused with `version_conflict` —
add a new file. `migrations` on a `frontend_only` app is refused at parse time. A hosted apply (one
the platform runs from a published blueprint) has no checkout, so the publisher ships the same files
on the app's built tree and the apply reads them from there; an artifact published before that
carries none and refuses the app by name — republish it, or run `naive up` from a clone.

A `fullstack` app's `buckets` are the buckets its [object store](/docs/cli/storage) must hold:
`[{ name: "avatars", public: true }, { name: "exports" }]`, names in the platform's bucket grammar
(3–63 lowercase letters, digits and hyphens), `public` defaulting to `false`. Each apply lists the
live buckets and creates the declared ones that are missing; one the app already holds is left
exactly as it is — `public` included, since flipping visibility on a bucket that is serving URLs is
a decision for a person — so the report says `2 bucket(s), 0 new` and the app is `unchanged` unless
one was made. Nothing is ever deleted here: a bucket dropped from the config, or made by the app's
own code, stays until `naive storage rb` removes it. `buckets` on a `frontend_only` app is refused
at parse time. With `--dry-run` the report says `will ensure buckets <names>`. Migrations run
before buckets, and both run after the app's secrets and deployment are written, whether `naive up`
applies from a clone or the platform applies a published blueprint in the background.

An agent's browser is declared where every tool is — `tools.configs.browser.config` — with the
[browser options](/docs/api/browser) the platform accepts (`allowed_domains`, `timeout_minutes`,
`context_name`, …), checked field by field at define time (above) and otherwise passed through
unchanged. **Computers, saved-login contexts and grants are not blueprint resources** and cannot be
declared: an agent opens its own computer, a saved-login context is what a live browser session
saves, and a grant names that context's id, so all three are made by running the agent (or with
`naive browser`), never by `up`.

A `vaults` entry provisions a credential vault by name, optionally held by a declared identity.
Credential values are real secrets, so they are `{ from_env }` **only** — never a literal — and are
read from your shell at apply time:

```ts theme={"system"}
vaults: [
  {
    name: "Ava's keys",
    identity: "Ava",
    credentials: [
      { kind: "static_bearer", key: "GitHub", mcp_server_url: "https://mcp.github.example/sse", value: { from_env: "GITHUB_TOKEN" } },
    ],
  },
],
```

Vault credentials are write-only and immutable on the platform, so `up` reconciles their
**presence**, not their value: a credential is identified by `(kind, key, host / mcp_server_url)`.
One that is live is `unchanged`, one that is missing is created (an unset `from_env` variable refuses
that one credential, naming the variable only, and never echoes a value), and credentials on the
vault that are not declared are never deleted or overwritten. Because a live value cannot be read or
replaced through `up`, **rotation is a manual operation**: create the new credential and delete the
old one on the platform (or with the SDK) — changing a `from_env` variable's value and re-running
`up` changes nothing. Each credential is a report line named `<vault> / <key>` under `vaults`; a
vault's `identity` cannot change after creation, so a live vault held by another identity is refused.

`env_var` credentials are refused at parse time: they need substitution at the sandbox egress
boundary, which the platform does not have, so the API would refuse them anyway — declare a
`static_bearer` or `mcp_oauth` credential with an `mcp_server_url` instead, which is injected
server-side before the sandbox sees it.

To delete a resource, move its name from the declaration into the config's `removed` block:

```ts theme={"system"}
export default defineProject({
  name: "my-project",
  agents: [/* … */],
  removed: {
    apps: ["old-dashboard"],
    agents: ["old-helper"],
    skills: ["old-skill"],
    identities: ["Old Persona"],
    vaults: ["Old Persona's keys"],
  },
});
```

`up` deletes each removed name it finds live and reports it as `deleted`; a name that is already
absent is `unchanged (already absent)`, so `removed` entries can stay in the config and re-running
stays safe. A name cannot be both declared and removed. Removing a vault deletes its credentials
with it.

**Renaming is a delete plus a create**: resources are keyed by name, so changing a declared name
mints a new resource and leaves the old one live — put the old name under `removed` in the same
apply, or it stays behind. **The config is the source of truth**: a field edited by hand in the
dashboard is drift, and the next `naive up` converges it back to what the config declares (a field
the config leaves out is never touched).

Two load failures stay distinct: a config that loaded but is wrong is reported as `config invalid`
(exit 2 — fix the file), while a config the toolchain could not evaluate (a missing install) is a
`config toolchain failure` (exit 1). A `.ts` config is evaluated with the CLI's own loader and
needs only the blueprint repo's install (`defineProject` comes from `@usenaive-sdk/blueprints`); a
`.json` config needs nothing installed at all.

## init

```bash theme={"system"}
naive init
naive init --force
```

| Flag | Description |
| - | - |
| `--force` | Overwrite an existing `naive.config.*`. Without it, an existing config is refused. |
| `--dir` | Where to write the scaffold (default: the current directory). |

## template

Clones a blueprint into a directory of its own. A blueprint is a public repository with a
`naive.config.ts` in it, so what you get is exactly what is on the branch — its screens, its server
and its tests — not a scaffold generated by string substitution. The git history is dropped: the
first commit of your company should be yours.

```sh theme={"system"}
naive template marketing-agency
cd marketing-agency
naive claim --key sk_...
naive up

# choose the crew as you clone
naive template media --template clipping
```

`--template` writes your choice into the clone's own `naive.config.ts`, so the next `naive up`
provisions that crew. Nothing else is fetched — the repository already carries every template its
blueprint has — and a template the blueprint does not have is refused before the clone.

| Flag | Default | |
| - | - | - |
| `--dir` | the blueprint's name | where to clone it |
| `--org` | `usenaive` | the GitHub organization to clone from, for a fork or a private mirror |
| `--template` | the blueprint's own default | which crew to provision (see [Blueprints and templates](#blueprints-and-templates)) |

## catalog

The published catalogue: one row per blueprint × template × version, carrying the setup questions
to ask first, the crew and apps that pair provisions, and the timers it runs.

```bash theme={"system"}
naive catalog
naive catalog --blueprint media --template clipping
```

| Flag | Description |
| - | - |
| `--blueprint` | Only this blueprint's rows. |
| `--template` | Only this template's rows. |
| `--limit` | Page size. |
| `--after` | Cursor from a previous page's `next_cursor`. |

Requires the `agents:read` scope. It reads and never applies — a published row becomes an install
when you clone the blueprint (`naive template`) and run `naive up`, which puts the tree in front of
you before it provisions a crew that costs money.

It answers the question `naive template` cannot: **which templates exist at which versions, right
now**, rather than which ones this binary was released knowing about. There is no catalogue inside
the CLI, deliberately — publishing a blueprint is publishing a repository and a row, not shipping a
new binary — so this is where the two meet.

## installs

One row per project this organization has applied: which blueprint and template, at which artifact
version, at which revision, and by which writer.

```bash theme={"system"}
naive installs --limit 20
naive installs --project faceless-media
```

| Flag | Description |
| - | - |
| `--project` | Only this project's row. |
| `--limit` | Page size. |
| `--after` | Cursor from a previous page's `next_cursor`. |

`naive up` reports the apply it just ran and nothing else. This reports what **anyone** applied,
which is the thing to read before an apply that expects a particular revision: an install the
dashboard advanced since you last ran `up` shows a higher `revision` here, and the row's `report`
carries what that apply did. A hosted apply the dashboard queued reads `status: "pending"` with
`report: null` until it has run; `--project` is how to watch one row until it says `applied` or
`failed`.

### installs remove

Take a template out of the company. Name the install by the id `naive installs` lists.

```bash theme={"system"}
naive installs remove bpi_0123456789abcdefghjkmnpqrs
```

Its agents are fired: their timers stop, and their open cards stay on the board with no one on
them. Its board tasks that are not done go, unless someone commented on them, and so do its mini
apps. A chat that is already running finishes first. Its apps and their data, its
personas and connected accounts, its skills, files and chats stay, and so does anything you or
another template made. Nothing is refunded or charged. Only the company's owner can do this, signed
in with `naive login --email`; an API key is refused. A second call answers `not_found`.

### installs context

What the crew of the project in this directory knows about the business it runs: the setup answers
with the questions they answer, the apps and their URLs, and the agents and their roles — the
**project context**, the same object a template agent reads through its `project_context` tool.

```bash theme={"system"}
naive installs context
naive installs context --set offer="Landing pages for B2B SaaS"
naive installs context --set channels=seo --set channels=email
naive installs context --clear reference
```

| Flag | Description |
| - | - |
| `--dir` | Directory holding the `naive.config.*` whose `name` is the project (default: the current directory). |
| `--set` | `key=value`: rewrite one setup answer. Repeat it for several answers, or for several values of a multiple choice. |
| `--clear` | `key`: put a setup answer back to unanswered. Only a question the template marked optional may be cleared. |

The project is the config's own `name`; its latest `applied` install is the one read, so a hosted
apply still `pending` is not it. Without `--set`, the context is printed. With `--set`, the edits
are laid over the install's stored answers and the whole set is written back — the platform
validates it against the template's questions, so an undeclared key is refused — and the context is
printed as the crew now reads it. A key set more than once, or a `multiple` choice set once, is a
list.

`--clear` is how an answer goes back to unanswered, and it is not the same as setting it to nothing:
an empty value is an answer, and the platform refuses one. A question the template marked optional is
answered by the key being absent, so `--clear` removes it rather than emptying it. Clearing a question
that is not optional is refused, because the crew would then be working to a company setting nobody
gave it.

An edit is not an apply: the install's `revision` does not move, nothing is re-provisioned and no
agent is briefed again. The crew simply reads the new answer the next time it looks. A project
with no applied install has no context yet: run `naive up` first. An install applied from a checkout
rather than from the catalogue is validated against the questions of the config it applied, and
`naive up` keeps its answers when it records the next apply. The record keeps only the config's
questions and its agents' names and roles — never its `env` values.

The repository is `<org>/<blueprint>-blueprint` — `naive template agency` clones
`usenaive/agency-blueprint` — so publishing a new blueprint is publishing a repository: there is no
catalogue inside this binary to drift from the blueprints that actually exist, and no release of the
CLI is needed to add one. The suffix is the convention a fork follows too, so `--org acme` looks for
`acme/agency-blueprint`. No API key is required: a blueprint is public, and claiming it comes after.

One blueprint isn't a repository: `support` ([Support Inbox](/docs/concepts/templates#support-inbox)) ships inside the
CLI. `naive template support` writes its `naive.config.json` instead of cloning, and `--org` is
refused for it.


# naive org
Source: https://usenaive.ai/docs/cli/org

Organizations, the active-org profile setting, and members.

An organization owns every other resource — agents, sessions, credits, keys. `naive login` writes the active org onto your profile from `GET /v1/me`; `--org org_…` overrides it for one command.

## Commands

| Command | Description |
| - | - |
| `naive org list` | Every organization this credential reaches. Needs no org id. |
| `naive org create` | Create an organization. Returns a working `admin` key, once. |
| `naive org use <org-id>` | Write an org id onto the active profile. |
| `naive org show [org-id]` | Show the active organization, or the one named. |
| `naive org update` | Rename the active organization, or set its timezone or logo. |
| `naive org members [org-id]` | List members of the active organization, or of the one named. |
| `naive org invite` | Invite a member by email with a role. |
| `naive org set-role <user-id>` | Change a member's role. |
| `naive org remove <user-id>` | Remove a member. |

> [!NOTE]
>
> Members are addressed by **`usr_` id**, not by email — `set-role` and `remove` take the id from `naive org members`. Only `invite` takes an email, because the user may not exist yet.

## list

```bash theme={"system"}
naive org list
```

```json theme={"system"}
{
  "data": [
    {
      "id": "org_gj9xg0gx6bpvdaysqvz68vr7b5",
      "object": "organization",
      "name": "acme-staging",
      "balance_micro_usd": 79416537,
      "created_at": "2026-08-21T12:05:48.146Z"
    }
  ],
  "has_more": false,
  "next_cursor": null
}
```

`list` and `create` are the two commands that need no org id. Everything else reads it from the profile (or `--org`), and with none there asks the credential itself (`GET /v1/me`), so a key in `NAIVE_API_KEY` is enough. `show` and `members` also take the org id on the line, which wins over `--org` and the profile. A credential that reaches no organization fails fast:

```
error: no organization on this profile or credential; run `naive login` or pass --org org_…
```

## create

```bash theme={"system"}
naive org create --name "Acme" --use
```

| Flag | Description |
| - | - |
| `--name` | Organization name (required). |
| `--use` | Also write the new org id onto the active profile. |

> [!WARNING]
>
> The reply carries a working `admin` API key for the new organization, and its secret appears **once**. Store it before the terminal scrolls; there is no way to read it back.

## use / show / update

```bash theme={"system"}
naive org use org_gj9xg0gx6bpvdaysqvz68vr7b5
naive org show
naive org update --name "Acme Inc"
naive org update --timezone America/Los_Angeles
naive org update --logo-file ./logo.svg
```

`update` takes `--name`, `--timezone` (an IANA name), `--logo-file` (a path to an SVG file), or any of
them together. The timezone is the company's: a routine created without one runs in it, and the
studio says when a post goes out in it. The logo shows in the studio's top-left corner and in its
apps; the API [checks it](/docs/api/organizations#the-logo) and says what to change when it refuses.

`show` returns the org record including its live credit balance:

```json theme={"system"}
{
  "id": "org_gj9xg0gx6bpvdaysqvz68vr7b5",
  "object": "organization",
  "name": "acme-staging",
  "balance_micro_usd": 79416537,
  "timezone": "America/New_York",
  "logo_svg": null,
  "created_at": "2026-08-21T12:05:48.146Z"
}
```

## members

```bash theme={"system"}
naive org members --limit 2
```

```json theme={"system"}
{
  "data": [
    {
      "id": "usr_hskm9b2nvg2egn9v9anddadr77",
      "object": "member",
      "email": "alice@example.com",
      "role": "member",
      "invited_by": "key_66nnedy98yfx3ygzssfv99p7tf",
      "created_at": "2026-08-22T16:24:07.077Z"
    }
  ],
  "has_more": true,
  "next_cursor": "usr_vptzsa5p9ayh3ykdsk5g3nmmz9"
}
```

| Flag | Description |
| - | - |
| `--limit` | Page size. |
| `--after` | Pagination cursor: the `next_cursor` of the previous page. |

## invite, set-role, remove

```bash theme={"system"}
naive org invite --email alice@acme.com --role admin
naive org set-role usr_hskm9b2nvg2egn9v9anddadr77 --role member
naive org remove usr_hskm9b2nvg2egn9v9anddadr77
```

| Flag | Description |
| - | - |
| `--email` | Invitee's email (`invite` only, required). |
| `--role` | `owner` \| `admin` \| `member`. Required by `invite` and `set-role`. |

`--role` is validated **client-side** against the shared role enum, so a typo fails before anything is sent rather than coming back as a 400.


# naive outcome
Source: https://usenaive.ai/docs/cli/outcomes

Create and read outcomes: a rubric a grader holds a session to.

Manage [outcomes](/docs/capabilities/outcomes) — a description of "done" plus a Markdown rubric, scored by a grader after each turn. An outcome is immutable: to change a rubric, create a new outcome.

## Commands

| Command | Description |
| - | - |
| `naive outcome create` | Create an outcome. |
| `naive outcome list` | List outcomes, newest first (paginated). |
| `naive outcome show <id\|name>` | Show one outcome, by `ocm_` id or by name. |
| `naive session outcome set` | Attach an outcome to an idle session ([sessions](/docs/cli/sessions#graded-against-an-outcome)). |

## create

```bash theme={"system"}
naive outcome create --name refund-quality \
  --description "A correct, policy-compliant refund." \
  --rubric-file ./rubrics/refund.md --max-iterations 4
```

| Flag | Description |
| - | - |
| `--name` | A label (required). Not unique; a name two outcomes share must be addressed by id. |
| `--description` | What a finished, correct result is (required). |
| `--rubric` | The rubric as inline Markdown. |
| `--rubric-file` | A local Markdown file, sent as the rubric's text — or an uploaded file's `fil_` id, read when the outcome is attached. |
| `--max-iterations` | Grade → revise rounds allowed. Default `3`, maximum `20`. |

Pass exactly one of `--rubric` and `--rubric-file`; both or neither exits `2` before anything is sent.

## list, show

```bash theme={"system"}
naive outcome list --limit 20
naive outcome show refund-quality
```

`show` and every `--outcome` flag take an `ocm_` id or a name. A name matching no outcome, or more than one, exits `2`.

## Attaching

```bash theme={"system"}
naive session create --agent agt_kt88353jaw132sjakt4sytz4a6 --outcome refund-quality --message "Refund order #4821"
naive session outcome set --session $SID --outcome refund-quality
naive session get $SID     # outcome_evaluations[]: result, iteration, explanation
```

There is no `naive outcome update` and no `naive outcome delete`: an evaluation names the rubric it was graded against.


# CLI overview
Source: https://usenaive.ai/docs/cli/overview

Install, authenticate, and learn the global conventions of the naive CLI.

The `naive` CLI is the primary way to operate Naive Managed Agents from a terminal, scripts, and CI. It defaults to machine-readable JSON so it composes with `jq`; pass `--human` for tables.

It is a thin shell over the [TypeScript SDK](/docs/sdk/typescript), which is a thin shell over the [API](/docs/api/overview) — one route table, three spellings. Every command below has a method with the same name and a page in the API reference.

## Install

```bash theme={"system"}
npm i -g @usenaive-sdk/cli
naive --version
```

> [!NOTE]
>
> Upgrading from `@usenaive-sdk/vetta-cli`? Run `npm rm -g @usenaive-sdk/vetta-cli` first, because both
> packages install the same commands. Your saved login carries over.

## Authenticate

```bash theme={"system"}
read -rs KEY && printf '%s\n' "$KEY" | naive login  # a scoped API key, piped on stdin
naive login --email you@acme.com --password ...    # person: exchanges for a session token
naive whoami                                       # show the active principal and organization
naive logout
```

There is no browser-based login. `naive login` takes an API key **piped on stdin** (recommended — it stays out of your shell history), from `NAIVE_API_KEY`, or from `--api-key`; **or** both `--email` and `--password`. The organization is learned from the credential, so you never pass an `org_` id. `naive login` on a new `--profile` points it at the production API unless you pass `--api-base-url`; other commands refuse a profile you never logged into. See [`naive auth`](/docs/cli/auth).

For CI, use an [API key](/docs/platform/organizations#api-keys) instead of an interactive login:

```bash theme={"system"}
export NAIVE_API_KEY=sk_live_...
naive whoami
```

Each setting is read from its flag first, then the environment, then the stored profile:

| Setting | Flag | Environment |
| - | - | - |
| API key | `--api-key` | `NAIVE_API_KEY` (the older `VETTA_API_KEY` is read only when `NAIVE_API_KEY` is unset) |
| Profile | `--profile` | `VETTA_PROFILE` |
| API base URL | `--api-base-url` | `VETTA_API_BASE_URL` |
| Organization | `--org` | `VETTA_ORG` |

A variable that is exported but empty counts as unset.

## Global flags

| Flag | Description |
| - | - |
| `--json` | Machine-readable JSON output (default). |
| `--human` | Human-friendly tables and colors. |
| `--org <id>` | Run against a specific organization. |
| `--api-key <key>` | Override the stored credential. |
| `--profile <name>` | Use a named credential profile. |
| `--api-base-url <url>` | Point at a different API deployment. |
| `--version` | Print the CLI and API versions. |
| `--help` | On a group, list its commands; on a command, list its flags. |

## Conventions

The CLI is consistent so command names transfer between groups:

* **Verbs & pluralization.** Resource groups are singular (`agent`, `session`, `webhook`); list/get/create/update/delete are the shared verbs; `members` live **under `org`** (`naive org members …`).
* **Ids** use the canonical `xxx_` prefixes on the wire (`agt_`, `ses_`, `cmp_`, `skl_`, `dep_`, `whk_`, `led_`, `key_`, `org_`, `usr_`).
* **Pause/resume vs enable/disable.** A *running* thing is paused/resumed (a computer sandbox, a deployment schedule). A *config flag* is enabled/disabled (a webhook endpoint). They never mix.
* **Unknown flags are an error.** A flag a command does not accept exits `2` before anything is sent, and the message lists the flags that command does take. A misspelled filter can never quietly widen your query.
* **Money.** `--budget-usd`, `--max-task-usd`, and `--usd` take decimal-dollar strings and convert client-side to integer micro-USD; JSON output amounts are integer `*_micro_usd` (`1 USD = 1_000_000` micro-USD).

## Command groups

The CLI's groups are below. `naive --help` prints them (with the top-level aliases below); `naive <group> --help` lists a group's commands; `naive <group> <command> --help` lists that command's flags.

| Group | Reference | What it does |
| - | - | - |
| `auth` | [naive auth](/docs/cli/auth) | Sign in, inspect the credential, sign out. |
| `agent` | [naive agent](/docs/cli/agents) | Create, version, roll back, and inspect agents. |
| `team` | [naive team](/docs/cli/team) | Compose a coordinator agent with a version-pinned roster. |
| `board` | [naive board](/docs/cli/board) | Read and move cards on a team's shared board. |
| `models` | [naive models](/docs/cli/models) | List the models an agent can run on. |
| `session` | [naive session](/docs/cli/sessions) | Create, send, stream, and manage runs. |
| `computer` | [naive computer](/docs/cli/computer) | Provision and control sandboxes, and drive a sandbox's browser (`naive computer browser`). |
| `browser` | [naive browser](/docs/cli/browser) | Saved logins that outlive a session, and who may reopen them. |
| `mobile` | [naive mobile](/docs/cli/mobile) | Cloud Android phones and iPhones: create, screenshot, tap and type, install apps, delete. |
| `data` | [naive data](/docs/cli/data) | Search the data catalogue, read a tool's input schema, and run it. |
| `social-data` | [naive social-data](/docs/cli/social-data) | The same catalogue's social domain: public social media data, no connected account. |
| `media` | [naive media](/docs/cli/media) | Generate images and video, cut clips, transcribe, speak; search models and stock photos. |
| `skill` | [naive skill](/docs/cli/skills) | Push and version skills. |
| `file` | [naive file](/docs/cli/files) | Upload inputs, download published outputs. |
| `app` | [naive app](/docs/cli/apps) | Hosted apps by hand, and the builds a project declaration provisioned. |
| `db` | [naive db](/docs/cli/database) | A fullstack app's database: SQL, tables, migrations. |
| `storage` | [naive storage](/docs/cli/storage) | A fullstack app's object store: buckets and objects. |
| `naive` | [naive](/docs/cli/naive) | Claim a blueprint repo and apply its `naive.config`. |
| `deploy` | [naive deploy](/docs/cli/deployments) | Schedule agents with cron. |
| `webhook` | [naive webhook](/docs/cli/webhook) | Subscribe endpoints; rotate secrets; inspect deliveries. |
| `org` | [naive org](/docs/cli/org) | Organizations and members. |
| `keys` | [naive keys](/docs/cli/keys) | Scoped API keys. |
| `plan` | [naive plan](/docs/cli/billing#the-plan) | The monthly plan (Standard or Pro) — the right to use the organization at all. |
| `credits` | [naive credits](/docs/cli/billing#the-balance) | Balance, top-ups, and the usage ledger. |
| `audit` | [naive audit](/docs/cli/audit) | The control-plane audit trail. |
| `proxy` | [naive proxy](/docs/api/proxy#from-the-cli) | The endpoint for a Messages-format client, and a one-shot call. |
| `identity` | [naive identity](/docs/cli/identity) | Personas, grants, and OAuth connections. |
| `domain` | [naive identity domain](/docs/cli/comms) | Sending/receiving domains. |
| `email` | [naive identity email](/docs/cli/comms) | Persona inboxes and messages. |
| `phone` | [naive identity phone](/docs/cli/phone) | Persona phone numbers and SMS. |
| `connections` | [naive identity connections](/docs/cli/identity#connections) | Connector auth configs. |
| `social` | [naive identity social](/docs/cli/social) | Social publishing for a persona. |
| `vault` | [naive vault](/docs/cli/vault) | Write-only credentials agents use but never see. |

`domain`, `email`, `phone`, `connections`, and `social` are reached as three-word `naive identity <group> <command>` spellings.

### Top-level aliases

`run`, `login`, `logout`, and `whoami` are shorthands for `session run`, `auth login`, `auth logout`, and `auth whoami`. `claim`, `template`, `up`, `init`, `catalog`, and `installs` are shorthands for the same commands under [`naive naive`](/docs/cli/naive) — `naive up` is `naive naive up`.

### Capabilities that are present but blocked

A command can exist and still be refused by something outside the platform. These are reported, not retried around:

| Surface | State |
| - | - |
| `naive identity phone send` | Refused `compliance_pending` until the carrier approves the number's messaging campaign. Inbound works throughout. |
| `naive identity email send` | Answers `501 feature_not_configured` where no comms provider is configured for the deployment. |

## Convenience: run

The `run` command is create-session + send + stream + wait-for-idle in one line. It exits with a code derived from the terminal `stop_reason` (non-zero on `awaiting_*`, `budget_paused`, `max_iterations`, `interrupted`, or `error`), so CI can branch on the outcome — see the [exit-code table](/docs/cli/sessions#run-exit-codes).

```bash theme={"system"}
naive run --agent agt_01j8rk2vq6m4zx9kp7n3c5hwae --message "Summarize what changed in main today" --window priority
```

## Declarative config (GitOps)

Agents are declarative, so you can keep them as checked-in **`.agent.yaml`** files and sync them from CI. `apply` upserts by name (last write wins); `show --format yaml` exports the live config for round-tripping.

```bash theme={"system"}
naive agent apply -f ./agents/            # sync every *.agent.yaml
```

See [Define an agent as a file](/docs/concepts/agents#define-an-agent-as-a-file).


# naive identity phone
Source: https://usenaive.ai/docs/cli/phone

Provision, list, update, release, and send from a persona's phone numbers.

Phone numbers belong to a [persona](/docs/cli/identity), so every command takes `--identity`. Reached as `naive identity phone <command>` — three words, where `phone` is a sub-group rather than a positional argument.

## Commands

| Command | Description |
| - | - |
| `naive identity phone provision` | Purchase a number for a persona. |
| `naive identity phone list` | List the persona's numbers. |
| `naive identity phone send` | Send an SMS as the persona. |
| `naive identity phone update` | Set or clear the agent a number's texts are for. |
| `naive identity phone release` | Release a number back to the pool. |

`--identity` takes either an `idn_` id or the persona's name; the API resolves both.

## provision

```bash theme={"system"}
naive identity phone provision --identity ava \
  --tier sole_prop --legal-name "<registered legal name>" --contact-phone +15555550123 --country US
```

`--legal-name` must be the legal name of the deployment's shared carrier registration; any other name is refused before anything is bought, because registering your own brand is not available yet. An organization holds at most 3 numbers.

| Flag | Description |
| - | - |
| `--identity` | Persona id or name (required; also accepted positionally). |
| `--tier` | `sole_prop` \| `standard` (required). |
| `--legal-name` | Registered legal name (required). |
| `--country` | ISO country code. |
| `--tax-id` | Required for `--tier standard`. |
| `--contact-phone` | Required for `--tier sole_prop`. Checked for shape only; no passcode is sent. |
| `--e164` | Request a specific number in E.164 form. |
| `--agent` | The agent inbound texts to this number are for (`owning_agent_id`), as an inbox names one for mail. |

> [!WARNING]
>
> **`provision` is a purchase**, and it answers `202`, not `201`. The number exists and can **receive** immediately, but outbound messaging waits on a carrier campaign decision that is not ours to make.

Neither `--tax-id` nor `--contact-phone` is stored or sent anywhere: numbers use the shared registration, so nothing is filed with them.

## list

```bash theme={"system"}
naive identity phone list --identity ava
```

