>
> How inbound email and SMS wake a sleeping agent.


# Social accounts
Source: https://usenaive.ai/docs/identity/social

Connect social accounts to a Naive Managed Agents identity and let its agent publish under policy.

Social accounts belong to an **identity**. If Ava and Billing are two identities in the same
organization, they activate and connect separate social workspaces. An agent can publish only when
its session selected the identity that owns those accounts.

The setup flow is short:

1. Activate Social for the identity with `POST /v1/identities/{id}/social/activate`.
2. Create a hosted portal link with `POST /v1/identities/{id}/social/portal`.
3. Give the returned URL to the person who owns the accounts.
4. Poll `GET /v1/identities/{id}/social/accounts`; it reads the provider's current state.

Naive Managed Agents never receives an OAuth token. It stores only which remote workspace belongs to the identity;
the provider holds and refreshes account grants.

The Worker must have `VETTA_SOCIAL_API_KEY` configured. This is the social publishing provider's
key, not the [connections](/docs/identity/connections) provider's. Without it, activation fails closed
with `feature_not_configured`.

## Agent tools

When a session selects an activated identity, its harness receives five tools:

* `social.accounts` lists connected accounts.
* `social.post` publishes or schedules a text post.
* `social.status` reads one published post's status and per-network analytics, by the id `social.post` returned.
* `social.post_metrics` reads how the organization's recent posts are doing, each metric against the identity's usual.
* `social.cancel` calls back a post the identity scheduled, by the id `social.post` returned, while it is more than
  two minutes from going out. It is offered wherever `social.post` is and asks first, even beside an allowed
  `social.post`; on a harness that cannot ask, it is offered only where the toolset allows it by name. There is
  no reschedule: to move a post, cancel it and post again with the new time, which is a second post fee. A
  cancelled post lists as `failed`, with the error "cancelled before it went out".

On the `pi` harness, every agent seated on the company board is also told, each turn, which accounts the company
has connected — the network and the handle, never an id — so a teammate that does not post itself knows the
account is there. A turn waits at most a few seconds for that list; an account the social layer cannot list in
time is left out of that turn.

`social.post` takes an opt-in `ai_generated`: a post that sets it carries each network's AI-content
label where it has one and ends its caption with `#AIgenerated`. Without it a post is unlabelled (see
[AI-generated posts](/docs/api/social#ai-generated-posts)).

`social.post` defaults to `ask`, including when the agent's default tool policy is `allow`. Set an
explicit policy for `social.post` if the agent should always be allowed or denied. A session with no
selected identity receives none of them.

Publishing supports text and URL-backed media on Bluesky, Facebook, LinkedIn, Mastodon, Threads,
and X. The account portal also connects Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, Pinterest, and Reddit. The API
can read account/post analytics and post comments, and can delete a post after verifying it belongs
to the identity's provider workspace.

> [card] [Social API](/docs/api/social)
>
> Activate a workspace, connect accounts, and publish text posts.


# Trading
Source: https://usenaive.ai/docs/identity/trading

Connect an identity's own brokerage account, and let its agents trade with a person approving each order.

An identity can connect **its own** brokerage account — `paper` (simulated money) or `live`, one of
each — over OAuth. An agent running a session as that identity can then read the account and quote,
and place an order, cancel one or close a position **only after a person approves that call**.

> [!WARNING]
>
> Naive Managed Agents is not a broker, a dealer or an investment adviser, and holds no customer money. The account, its orders and its fills belong to the brokerage and the person who owns it. Nothing Naive or an agent says about a symbol is investment advice, and an agent can be wrong. Start on `paper`.

## Connecting

1. Start the authorization from the identity's page in the dashboard (**Brokerage → Connect**), with
   [`naive trading connect`](/docs/cli/trading), or with
   [`POST /v1/identities/{id}/trading/connect`](/docs/api/trading#connect).
2. Read the consent text shown first — every surface shows it before the link — then open the link and
   approve at the brokerage. The link works once and expires after 15 minutes.
3. The brokerage sends the browser back to the identity's page, which says whether it connected. The
   connection is now `active`.

A connection belongs to the identity, never to an agent or the organization: an agent reaches a
brokerage only through the identity its session selected. Connecting and disconnecting need a key
with `billing:write`; connecting a `live` account also needs a live `sk_live_` key.

Naive keeps one **sealed** access token per identity and env. No response, log or audit entry carries
it, and it is never placed in an agent's computer, so an agent cannot reach the brokerage around the
approval below. When the brokerage revokes access the connection turns `expired`: connect again.
**Disconnect** deletes the token; revoking Naive at the brokerage too is done in its own settings.

## In the dashboard

The identity's page has a **Brokerage** panel: each env's state (with the reason on a failed one),
Connect, Reconnect or Disconnect, and — for an active account — its open positions and open orders,
read-only. Orders are placed by an agent, the [API](/docs/api/trading#place-an-order) or the
[CLI](/docs/cli/trading), never from the panel.

## Agent tools

A session whose identity has an `active` connection is offered:

| Tool | What it does | Default policy |
| - | - | - |
| `trading.account` | Cash, buying power and equity. | the agent's default |
| `trading.positions` | Open positions. | the agent's default |
| `trading.orders` | Orders by status, or one order by `order_id`. | the agent's default |
| `trading.quote` | Latest bid and ask for one or more symbols. | the agent's default |
| `trading.place_order` | Place an order. | **ask** |
| `trading.cancel_order` | Cancel an open order. | **ask** |
| `trading.close_position` | Close a position, in full or in part. | **ask** |

The three writes name the account (`env`) on every call. By default each one pauses the session on an approval
card that says, in plain words, the account, symbol, side, size, type and any limit or stop price;
nothing reaches the brokerage until a person approves, and a decline sends nothing. An approval
covers that one call — it cannot be granted for the rest of a chat.

**The live account always asks.** An operator may set a write tool to `allow` in the agent's
[policy](/docs/concepts/policies); that is honoured only for a call whose `env` is `paper`. A call on the
`live` account — or one that does not say — still waits for a person. A surface that cannot pause a
call does not offer the writes at all.

An approved order is placed exactly once, even if the session is retried after the approval: the call
carries a stable `client_order_id`.

## What is not here

Opening or funding a brokerage account, trailing stops, bracket orders, historical prices, streaming
and watchlists. Order kinds placed elsewhere that Naive does not offer are left out of its lists.
Trading is not billed by Naive.


# Credential vault
Source: https://usenaive.ai/docs/identity/vault

Secrets injected at the network boundary — the agent never sees raw values.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Available now.** The vault API and CLI are live, with write-only at-rest encryption. Injection is live on the [MCP connector](/docs/capabilities/tools#mcp-connector) path.

> [!WARNING]
>
> **`env_var` credentials are not available.** Creating one answers `501 feature_not_configured` and nothing is stored: the egress boundary that would substitute the value does not exist yet. Use `static_bearer` or `mcp_oauth`, which are injected before the sandbox sees the token.

The vault lets you register a credential once and reference it by ID, so you don't run your own secret store or transmit tokens on every call. Its defining property: **the agent never sees the raw secret**. Values are injected at the network boundary, so nothing sensitive enters the model's context, the transcript, or your logs.

## Setting a credential

```bash CLI theme={"system"}
# one vault per identity (by id or name); credentials are sealed into it by vault id
naive vault create --name ava-secrets --identity ava

# MCP static bearer, keyed by server URL; the value is read from stdin, never echoed
naive vault set --vault vlt_... --mcp-bearer https://mcp.example.com/mcp

# MCP OAuth token
naive vault set --vault vlt_... --mcp-oauth https://chat.example.com/mcp
naive vault credentials --vault vlt_...   # metadata only; no value is ever returned
naive vault rm --vault vlt_... --credential vcr_...
```

```typescript TypeScript theme={"system"}
const vault = await client.vaults.create({ display_name: "ava-secrets", identity_id: "idn_..." });
await client.vaults.credentials.create(vault.id, {
  kind: "static_bearer",
  key: "Task tracker API key",
  value: "tok_...",
  mcp_server_url: "https://mcp.example.com/mcp",
});
```

## How network-boundary injection works

```
mcp_oauth / static_bearer:
  MCP connector (server-side)  injects the token when the agent connects to mcp_server_url
```

The token is added on our side of the connection, matched to the exact `mcp_server_url` it was stored for. The sandbox process, the model, the transcript, and logs never see it, and no other server URL receives it.

## At rest

Credentials are protected with envelope encryption: a per-write data key wraps the value with AES-256-GCM, and the data key itself is wrapped by a key held in a managed key service, bound to the org and identity. A vault maps to an [identity](/docs/identity/overview) and is referenced per session.

## Credential kinds

**env\_var** `credential`

**Not available.** Refused with `501 feature_not_configured`. It is meant for CLIs and direct API calls that read an environment variable, with the real value substituted at egress only for one bound `host`; that egress boundary does not exist yet, so nothing is stored.

**mcp\_oauth** `credential`

For MCP servers that use OAuth 2.0, keyed by `mcp_server_url`. The access token is the `value`, injected server-side when the agent connects. There is no refresh: rotate by adding a new credential and deleting the old one.

**static\_bearer** `credential`

For MCP servers that accept a fixed bearer token (API key or PAT), keyed by `mcp_server_url`. No refresh needed.

An MCP credential can also be **bound to one agent** with `agent_id`. It is then injected into that agent's sessions only, even when another agent declares the same server. A credential for this platform's own `/v1/mcp` is never injected: bound, it marks the agent as your organization's CEO, which gets a short-lived credential for each turn holding only what the people driving it may do. Binding makes the agent an admin's to change: editing, rolling back or deleting it needs the `admin` scope. A version older than the binding gets the credential only while it is the agent's current version.

The secret travels in one field, `value`, which is **write-only** and never returned by the API. Reads return metadata only. An `expires_at` must be in the future; a past one is refused with `400 validation_failed`.

> [card] [Back to identity](/docs/identity/overview)
>
> How personas tie it all together.


# Wallet
Source: https://usenaive.ai/docs/identity/wallet

A custodied, spend-limited wallet an identity carries so its agent can pay for things in the world.

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Coming soon · not available yet (Phase 5).** The agent wallet is not offered to customers yet, as the [identity overview](/docs/identity/overview) says. The reference below describes the planned surface; do not build on it yet, and expect `501 feature_not_configured` where it is not enabled. There is no delete: a wallet is retired by `sweep`.

A wallet belongs to an **identity** — at most one live wallet per identity **per network**. It holds
USDC on Base (the test network by default; mainnet is enabled per organization by its owner) at a
custody provider that keeps the key: Naive Managed Agents holds the public address, the policy and the ledger, and
asks the provider to sign. An agent can spend only when its session selected the identity that owns
the wallet.

## Testnet and mainnet

Every identity starts on the test network (`eip155:84532`, funded from a faucet). Once the
organization's owner has enabled mainnet, the same identity may hold a second wallet on Base
(`eip155:8453`) with real USDC. The two wallets are independent — separate address, balance, caps,
frozen state and ledger — and every surface says which one it means: `?network=` on the API, a
trailing `{ network }` in the SDK, `--network base-testnet | base` in the CLI, an optional `network`
on the agent tools, and a **Testnet | Mainnet** switch at the top of the wallet page. Nothing ever
falls back to the other network: with Mainnet selected the page shows the mainnet wallet or an
empty state to create one, never the testnet balance, and a sibling transfer lands in the
recipient's wallet on the sender's network or is refused.

## Wallet vs. credits — two different moneys

| | [Credits / billing](/docs/platform/billing) | Wallet |
| - | - | - |
| What it pays for | Managed Agents usage — inference, compute, browser, storage | **External** resources the agent buys |
| Who is paid | Managed Agents | Third parties, over the x402 protocol or by transfer |
| Denomination | Credits on the organization | USDC held for the identity, in integer micro-USD |
| Guardrail | [Budgets](/docs/concepts/budgets) priced per call | Per-transaction and daily caps, freeze, approvals |

The two never draw from each other: a short wallet balance is `validation_failed`, never
`insufficient_credits`.

## How it works

1. `POST /v1/identities/{id}/wallet` provisions the wallet. The policy — per-transaction cap
   (default \$0.50), daily cap — is attached at the provider **before** the wallet exists.
2. Fund it with `POST …/wallet/fund`: the test faucet (testnet only, a fixed 1 USDC per request)
   or the organization's treasury once the owner has provisioned one.
3. The agent probes a paywalled URL with `wallet.quote` (no side effects) and pays with
   `wallet.pay`, which spends the smaller of its request ceiling and the per-transaction cap,
   reserves the daily budget, retries the request with the payment attached and records a receipt.
   Each tool takes an optional `network` and works on the testnet wallet without one.
4. Every fund, transfer, payment and sweep is a `wallet_transaction` under
   `GET …/wallet/transactions`; receipts are `?kind=pay`.
5. `freeze` stops spending at the provider; `sweep` drains the balance and retires the wallet as
   `swept`. A retired wallet stays in the ledger and a fresh one may be provisioned in its place.

The caps are enforced twice: the provider refuses to sign any payment above the per-transaction cap
(so a cap holds even if Managed Agents is wrong), and Managed Agents' own durable daily counter refuses a spend that
would cross the daily cap before anything is signed. A wallet's balance is read live from the
provider on every read; Managed Agents never caches it.

## Agent tools

`wallet.balance`, `wallet.transactions`, `wallet.receipts` and `wallet.quote` are reads and run
under the agent's ordinary policy. `wallet.pay` and `wallet.transfer` default to `ask`, including
when the agent's default tool policy is `allow`: the session pauses, the operator sees the URL or
the recipient and the amount in micro-USD, and nothing is signed until they approve. Provisioning,
policy, funding and sweeping are operator actions with no tool.

The tools work on the wallet of the identity the session selected, and only when the deployment
has a custody provider bound — otherwise the agent simply has no wallet tools. Each tool answers the
same safe projection the API does: an address, a policy, a ledger, never a key.

## In a blueprint

```ts theme={"system"}
identities: [
  { name: "Ava", wallet: { network: "eip155:84532", policy: { per_tx_cap_micro_usd: 500_000, daily_cap_micro_usd: 20_000_000 } } },
  {
    name: "Bea",
    wallet: [
      { policy: { per_tx_cap_micro_usd: 500_000 } }, // testnet
      { network: "eip155:8453", policy: { per_tx_cap_micro_usd: 250_000 } },
    ],
  },
],
```

Each declaration is the body of `POST /v1/identities/{id}/wallet` — one object, or a list with at
most one per network. `naive up` creates the wallet on that network if the identity has none there
and patches `policy` when a declared cap differs; it never funds, freezes or sweeps one, a frozen
wallet's policy is refused until it is unfrozen, and a wallet on a network the declaration does not
name is never read or touched. A mainnet declaration reports as `Ava / wallet eip155:8453`.

> [card] [Wallet API](/docs/api/wallet)
>
> Provision, cap, fund, transfer, sweep, and pay for paywalled resources.


# Naive docs
Source: https://usenaive.ai/docs/index

The most efficient managed agent for long-horizon work. The highest intelligence per dollar, by design.

**Naive Managed Agents is a managed agent platform**: you define an [agent](/docs/capabilities/agent) — model, prompt, tools, skills, budget — and run it as [sessions](/docs/concepts/sessions) that work for hours, pause at storage cost, and finish without a person in the loop. You pay per finished task, in real dollars, priced before each call runs.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Two layers, one stack.** Naive Managed Agents is the autonomous-company infrastructure — the harness, the managed runtime, sessions, budgets, tools. Naive **blueprints** are the layer on top: the templates a whole company is installed from, and the [studio](https://app.usenaive.ai) you run it in. These pages are the Managed Agents reference.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Why you'll see `vetta`.** A few API identifiers still carry the old name, including the `api.vetta.sh` host and the `Vetta-Version` header. They're the same product as Naive.

Everything is built around one number: **the most intelligence per dollar spent** — the same model on different stacks varies several-fold in cost per completed task ([benchmarks](https://usenaive.ai/blogs/introducing-naive-managed-agents)).

![Naive Managed Agents — managed agents infrastructure: any model and provider, skills, and tools in; harness, runtime, orchestration, and self-improvement inside; run and interact through the Web Studio, API, CLI, and SDK](https://mintcdn.com/vetta/U1iUpSFRnmMwfSsJ/images/architecture-overview.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=U1iUpSFRnmMwfSsJ\&q=85\&s=fe760fd7f5f313494ae586505b409791)

Any model, your skills, and your tools go in; Managed Agents' runtime does the work; and you run and interact through the [Web Studio](https://app.usenaive.ai), the [API](/docs/api/overview), the [CLI](/docs/cli/overview), or the [SDK](/docs/sdk/typescript).

## Create an agent, run a session

```typescript TypeScript theme={"system"}
// ESM only: set "type": "module" in package.json, or name the file .mts
import { createClient } from "@usenaive-sdk/managed-agents";

const naive = createClient({ baseUrl: "https://api.vetta.sh", apiKey: process.env.NAIVE_API_KEY! });

const agent = await naive.agents.create({
  name: `triage-${Date.now()}`,
  model: "z-ai/glm-5.3-flash",
  system: "You are a concise triage agent.",
  budget: { cap_micro_usd: 50_000_000, max_task_micro_usd: 5_000_000, period: "month" },
});

const session = await naive.sessions.create({
  agent_id: agent.id,
  message: "Summarize what changed in main overnight.",
});

for await (const event of naive.stream(session.id)) {
  console.log(event.type);
}
```

```bash CLI theme={"system"}
npm i -g @usenaive-sdk/cli
read -rs KEY && printf '%s\n' "$KEY" | naive login   # piped: the key stays out of argv and shell history

AGENT=$(naive agent create --name triage --model z-ai/glm-5.3-flash \
  --budget-usd 50 --max-task-usd 5 --budget-period month \
  --system "You are a concise triage agent." | jq -r .id)

SID=$(naive session create --agent "$AGENT" \
  --message "Summarize what changed in main overnight." | jq -r .id)

naive session stream --session "$SID"
```

# Credits & billing
Source: https://usenaive.ai/docs/platform/billing

A real US-dollar balance, topped up through the payments provider, metered against vendor cost.

Naive Managed Agents billing is **real US dollars** — no abstract point currency. Your organization holds a balance; every action draws from it at metered cost.

## The balance

Your [organization](/docs/platform/organizations) has one balance, denominated in US dollars. Every agent it owns draws from the same balance.

```bash CLI theme={"system"}
naive credits show
naive credits ledger --limit 50     # every grant and charge
```

## Topping up

Add funds through a hosted checkout session with the payments provider. You can also set up a subscription that grants a monthly dollar allowance.

```bash CLI theme={"system"}
naive credits topup --usd 50        # returns a checkout link
naive credits show                  # current balance
naive credits ledger --limit 20     # what the balance was spent on
```

```typescript TypeScript theme={"system"}
const checkout = await naive.credits.topup({ usd: 50 });
console.log(checkout.url);
```

## How usage is metered

Costs are measured against **vendor invoices**, not list price, and drawn from the balance in real dollars. What you see quoted is what you are charged — see the [rate card](/docs/platform/pricing).

* **[Model calls](/docs/concepts/model-router)** — per token across five tiers, at the [completion window](/docs/concepts/completion-window) tariff.
* **[Computer](/docs/computer/limits-and-billing)** — a computer you create is billed ahead in 10-minute blocks while running, a session's per running second; paused bills nothing; no creation fee.
* **[Priced tools](/docs/platform/pricing#priced-tools)** — [`web_search`/`web_fetch`](/docs/capabilities/tools#web-tools) per call, [`generate_image`/`generate_video`](/docs/capabilities/tools#generation-tools) per finished job.

![Quote before spend: every call is priced, checked against the budget cap and org balance, then either runs with an idempotent ledger entry or is refused with budget\_paused and nothing spent](https://mintcdn.com/vetta/rjfQyQrWaQ5bFTTq/images/quote-before-spend.svg?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=rjfQyQrWaQ5bFTTq\&q=85\&s=3d84f1c0ee3fd78de9de066afa0be56b)

Every charge is:

1. **Quoted before the call** and checked against your [budget](/docs/concepts/budgets) and balance.
2. **Recorded as an idempotent ledger entry** — the balance can never be double-charged for the same call.
3. **Floored at zero** — the wallet never goes negative; a small post-hoc overshoot is forgiven rather than clawed back.

## Reading spend

```bash CLI theme={"system"}
naive agent spend agt_01j8rk2vq6m4zx9kp7n3c5hwae --by component   # model vs computer vs search vs media
naive session get $SID                  # cost consumed by one run
```

Every ledger debit records the [5-tier token line items](/docs/concepts/model-router), the `session_id`, and the acting `actor`, so spend is attributable end to end.

> [!NOTE]
>
> Managed Agents meters against measured vendor cost because list-price rate cards over-state real cost by 1.017x–4.176x depending on harness and window — see [Benchmarks](https://usenaive.ai/blogs/introducing-naive-managed-agents).

## Attribution & live usage

* **Who spent it** — every action and money movement is principal-attributed; see the [audit log](/docs/api/audit-logs).
* **Live cost per run** — a session exposes `consumed_micro_usd` and 5-tier `token_usage`, and emits `session.usage` before idle. See [Observability](/docs/capabilities/observability).

## On the wire

Money is integer **micro-USD** (`_micro_usd`, `1 USD = 1_000_000`) everywhere on the wire — every ledger entry, session `consumed_micro_usd`, and quote. The CLI renders dollars for humans.

> [card] [Next: pricing & the completion window](/docs/platform/pricing)
>
> How the window changes what you pay.


# Organizations & members
Source: https://usenaive.ai/docs/platform/organizations

The organization is the billing entity; users are members.

Everything in Naive Managed Agents belongs to an **organization** — the billing entity that holds the credit balance and owns every agent, computer, skill, and identity. Users are **members**.

## Model

```
organization  (billing entity, owns everything)
├── members            users with a role: owner | admin | member
├── api keys           programmatic access, org-scoped
├── credit balance     real US dollars
├── agents             each with its own budget
├── computers
├── skills
├── files
└── identities
```

## Roles

| Role | Can do |
| - | - |
| `owner` | Everything, including deleting the company. Only an owner can make someone an owner, or change or remove one. A company keeps at least one who has joined. The exception is a company with no such owner yet, so one made with an API key can get its first. |
| `admin` | Everything else: invite and remove people, manage keys, billing, agents and computers. |
| `member` | Create and run agents with the company's resources, and connect their own agent. |

## Your agent

Anyone in a company can connect an agent they run elsewhere, such as their own coding agent, from **Members → Connect your agent**. They paste the result into its MCP settings.

* It works as its person. Its messages show as theirs, and Members shows "Agent connected" on their row.
* It stops at its next call if its person leaves.
* It holds a member's access whatever its person's role, so an owner's agent cannot manage people, keys or billing, and cannot approve what always asks a person.
* It can do what a member can: run agents and computers, send messages, deploy apps and spend the company's balance. There is no per-person limit yet, so treat what you paste like a password.
* It lasts 90 days, then you connect it again. Its person can disconnect it sooner, and so can any owner or admin, from the person's menu.

## Inviting someone

An invite emails them a link. Until they sign in, Members shows them as **Invited**, and you can send it again or cancel it. An invited owner counts as an owner only once they've joined.

## Who said what

A company's chats are shared. A message from someone else shows who sent it, and your own stays as it was. Messages sent before this existed show no name.

Only a key's own person or an owner can rotate it, because rotating hands over its secret. An admin can revoke anyone's key.

## When someone leaves

Removing someone ends their sign-in and their connected agents, and revokes the API keys and MCP sessions they made, including keys those keys made. It happens in one step, so nothing minted at that moment can slip past. Moving an owner or admin down to `member` revokes the same keys and sessions, and leaves their connected agents working. A revoked key can keep reading and running for up to 3 seconds while servers drop it from their cache, but it can't mint another credential or change the team.

Some things stay, because they are the company's: an app's own key, webhooks, deployments, vault credentials, and anyone they invited. If you don't trust how someone left, check those, and rotate app keys. Chats they drove lose the CEO's tools.

## Managing an organization

```bash CLI theme={"system"}
naive org create --name "Acme"
naive org list
naive org use <org_id>              # set the active org for subsequent commands
naive org invite --email alice@acme.com --role admin
naive org members                   # members are addressed by their usr_ id
naive org set-role usr_... --role member
```

```typescript TypeScript theme={"system"}
const org = await naive.orgs.create({ name: "Acme" });
await naive.orgs.addMember(org.id, { email: "alice@acme.com", role: "admin" });
```

## API keys

Programmatic access uses org-scoped API keys. Keys can carry scopes to limit what they can do.

A company created by a signed-in customer is `live`, because customer onboarding continues directly
to subscription checkout — Standard with its 7-day free trial, or Pro ([Plans](/docs/platform/pricing#plans)). Keys created inside it therefore use the `sk_live_…` prefix. A company
created by an API key inherits that key's mode, so an `sk_test_…` credential cannot mint live access.

```bash CLI theme={"system"}
naive keys create --name ci --scopes agents:write,sessions:write
naive keys list
naive keys revoke <key_id>
```

> [!WARNING]
>
> An API key is shown once at creation. Store it securely; it cannot be retrieved again.

## Compliance & tenancy

| Area | Today | Roadmap |
| - | - | - |
| **Tenancy** | Logical multi-tenancy: every organization's data is isolated per-org and scoped by org id on every request. | Dedicated single-tenant deployment is not offered yet. |
| **Data residency** | All organization data is stored in Managed Agents' primary region. | Region pinning is planned. |
| **Certifications** | None claimed yet. | SOC 2 Type II and related attestations are on the roadmap. |
| **Data handling** | Secrets are held in the [vault](/docs/identity/vault) and injected at the network boundary; transcripts and files are org-scoped and retained per plan. | Configurable retention windows. |

> [!NOTE]
>
> Roadmap items above are planned, not shipped — if one is a hard requirement for your deployment, contact us before building on it.

## Bootstrapping

Signing up creates your organization, adds you as `owner`, and opens a credit balance in one step. Default resources are created lazily on first use.

> [card] [Next: credits & billing](/docs/platform/billing)
>
> How real-dollar credits and billing work.


# Pricing
Source: https://usenaive.ai/docs/platform/pricing

What you pay, and how the completion window changes it.

Naive Managed Agents charges for what your agents actually consume, in real dollars — no per-seat fee. The one recurring charge is the [plan](/docs/cli/billing#the-plan), per organization, and each paid month grants credit equal to its price toward that consumption.

## Plans

| Plan | Price | Included credit | Free trial |
| - | - | - | - |
| **Standard** | \$20 per month | \$20 each paid month | 7-day free trial |
| **Pro** | \$200 per month | \$200 each paid month | — |
| **Custom** | Talk to us | — | — |

Both plans run the same platform at the same published rates; the only difference is the credit each paid month includes.

* **The 7-day free trial** is on Standard only. A card is required to start it, the trial grants $10 of credit (none on a prepaid card, a card whose security-code check fails or cannot run, or a card that already started a trial), and unless you cancel before it ends it converts to $20 per month with the full \$20 of credit. One trial per organization and one per person.
* **Included credit rolls over.** It is added to your organization's prepaid balance alongside anything you top up, and it never expires.
* **Upgrade to Pro any time** from the Credits page, under Settings → Credits (or [`naive plan change --plan pro`](/docs/cli/billing#plan-change)). It takes effect at once: the difference for the rest of the month is charged now, and upgrading during the trial ends the trial and charges \$200.
* **Moving back to Standard** takes effect at the end of the month already paid for. Nothing is refunded and the Pro credit already granted stays in the balance.

## What you pay for

| Component | How it's priced |
| - | - |
| **Plan** | Standard $20 per month or Pro $200 per month, per organization, each including its price back as credit every paid month — see [Plans](#plans). Every route outside billing needs one — see [`naive plan`](/docs/cli/billing#the-plan). |
| **Model inference** | Per token across a five-tier ledger, at the request's [completion window](/docs/concepts/completion-window) tariff. See [Model router](/docs/concepts/model-router). |
| **Computer** | Per-second vCPU + memory while running. **No creation fee**; nothing at all while paused. |
| **Web tools** | [`web_search` and `web_fetch`](/docs/capabilities/tools#web-tools), per call, and [`data_run`](/docs/capabilities/tools#built-in-tools), per run — [rates below](#priced-tools). |
| **Media generation** | [`generate_image`, `generate_video` and `clip_video`](/docs/capabilities/tools#generation-tools), [`generate_3d_model`](/docs/capabilities/3d), [`transcribe_audio`, `generate_speech`, `generate_sound_effect` and `generate_music`](/docs/capabilities/tools#audio-tools), and the [Clips API](/docs/api/clips), per finished job; [`create_character`](/docs/capabilities/tools#characters) and [`POST /v1/characters`](/docs/api/characters), per training — [rates below](#priced-tools). |
| **Browser** | The [managed browser](/docs/computer/browser), per session minute open to close plus a fixed price per model-driven action — [rates below](#priced-tools). |
| **Voice calls** | A hands-free voice call over a chat, per started minute from connect to hang-up — [rate below](#priced-tools). The words and replies are the chat's, billed as model inference as usual. |
| **Email** | Each outbound [email](/docs/identity/email) an identity sends, `$0.0008` per send however many recipients it has. Booked after the provider accepts it; a send the balance cannot cover is refused with `402 insufficient_credits`. |
| **Mobile sandbox** | A [cloud Android phone or iPhone](/docs/computer/mobile), per phone-minute from create to end. **No creation fee** — [rates below](#priced-tools). |
| **Storage** | A fullstack app's [object storage](/docs/api/storage), per bucket per day — **no rate is published yet, so nothing is booked**. |

> [!NOTE]
>
> Every rate published here and on [Limits & billing](/docs/computer/limits-and-billing) is **the price you pay** — the number the [ledger](/docs/platform/billing) books and the number your spend breakdown reports. There is no separate fee, no seat charge and no minimum on top of it.

## Priced tools

Several tool families have a price of their own, on top of the tokens the model spends calling them. Each appears on `GET /v1/agents/{id}/spend?by=component` under its own component name. An app's [database](/docs/api/database) is not one of them: `/v1/apps/{id}/db/*` calls and the `apps` tool's `db_*` actions carry no price of their own.

**They are all booked after the fact.** A web call is priced from what the provider charged for it, so the debit lands **after** the call: an agent already at its cap can still make one. Media is the same — nothing is reserved before a render (see below), so `max_task_micro_usd` does **not** bound one; a character training is the one media job held first. Watch the `search` and `media` components to see what each is costing, and treat the agent's `cap_micro_usd` and the organization's balance as the real limits.

### Web tools — per call, `search` component

| Call | Price |
| - | - |
| `web_search` — one query, up to 10 results | `$0.00166` |
| `web_fetch` — one page read as text | `$0.00083` |
| `data_run` (`POST /v1/data/runs`) — one run | The tool's listed price |
| `POST /v1/social_data/runs` — one run | The tool's listed price |

The listed price is the price you pay: `data_search`, `data_describe` and `GET /v1/social_data/tools` report it. The median per-call data tool is about `$0.0015`, seven in ten cost `$0.01` or less, and the most expensive is about `$0.95`; most social data tools are `$0.003` per call. Some tools are priced per result, at most 25 results per run.

Data and social data runs are the exception to booking after the fact: a run is **admitted first**, capped at 25 results and admitted at its most it can cost — through the API, the balance must cover the tool's listed price for one call (or for 30 results on a per-result tool, since some sources bill results in blocks of 10), else `402 insufficient_credits`; from an agent, the run takes a hold against the session's budget. A data or social data run that fails — refused input, a network error — is not charged. A run past its two-minute limit is stopped and normally not charged; one the source meters per result costs what it gathered before the stop. Searching for and describing a data or social data tool is free.

A search whose results are all filtered out by the agent's [domain policy](/docs/capabilities/tools#web-tools) still costs the call — the query ran. A `web_fetch` refused by that policy is stopped **before** the page is requested and costs nothing; a page that *redirected* somewhere the policy forbids is withheld after the fetch, and that one is billed, because the fetch happened.

### Media generation — per finished job, `media` component

You are billed **what the finished job actually cost**, once per job.

There is no per-model price table here, and that is deliberate rather than an omission. A generation job's cost depends on the model, the duration and the size, and the catalogue changes without a release of ours — so a table on this page would be stale the day a model is added. A video on a model priced per generated second costs its length at the resolution it renders at (720p on the platform's per-second models, unless it says otherwise); every other job costs what its model reported for it. What can be listed is which models exist: [`GET /v1/media/models`](/docs/api/media), read live from the provider. The [audio](/docs/api/audio) routes and tools are on this component too: a transcription costs what the provider charged for the recording, speech what it charged for the characters spoken (the default speech model runs on our own servers and costs $0.000029 a second of audio, $0.00174 a minute), and a [sound effect](/docs/api/audio#sound-effects) what it charged for the seconds generated, and a [song](/docs/api/audio#music) the same, for the seconds of music generated.

**Nothing is reserved for an image or a video before it renders.** Most renders cannot be priced before they run, and a ceiling is not a price, so no hold is taken against the agent's [budget](/docs/concepts/budgets) and no balance floor is checked, from a session or over REST. The real cost is booked once, when the job lands, on the render's own idempotency key; a render costs cents, and a balance may go negative by one rather than turn the request away. A job that fails or never finishes is not billed at all.

**A character training is held first and billed once.** [`create_character`](/docs/capabilities/tools#characters) takes a hold against the session's budget before anything is bought — a budget with no room refuses it — and asks by default. Over REST, the prepaid balance must cover one training first (`402 insufficient_credits` otherwise). The training, from a session or [over REST](/docs/api/characters#billing), is billed once, on the media component, when the trainer accepts the photos; a request refused before then is not billed, and a training that later ends `failed` is refunded, on the read that sees it fail. A replay under the same key charges nothing.

**An edit with Mira (`edit_video`) has a set price, and is held.** An edit with no photos costs $0.03 per second of the source clip, rounded up to whole seconds, at 720p; clips are trimmed to 15 s, so it costs at most $0.45. An edit with photos, or a person swap, is \$1.48 at any length, at 1080p. The price is held against the agent's budget at submit: the clip's own length when it is known, else 15 s. Every finished edit is billed, including one you asked for again. An edit that fails, is refused, times out, or is cancelled while queued costs nothing.

**A clipping job submitted over REST has no agent, so no reservation.** [`POST /v1/media/clips`](/docs/api/clips#pricing) is admitted while the prepaid balance is above zero (`402 insufficient_credits` otherwise), and what it can cost is bounded server-side instead: the input is capped at 90 minutes of video and every metered actual the job reports is clamped before it is priced. The debit lands once, on completion; a failed job bills nothing.

### 3D assets

A generated 3D model ([`generate_3d_model`](/docs/capabilities/3d), [`POST /v1/media/meshes`](/docs/api/meshes)) is one charge for the finished model. The amount depends only on which model ran and on `texture` and `rig`. Render time, file size and polygon count leave it unchanged. It is booked on the `media` component when the job completes; a failed job is free. [`GET /v1/media/models?kind=mesh`](/docs/api/media) lists that charge for every option, as `prices[].micro_usd`.

| Finished model | Charge |
| - | - |
| From a photo, fast model, untextured | `$0.20` |
| From a photo (or 2–4 views), fast model, textured | `$0.30` |
| From a photo, detailed model | `$0.50` |
| From a description, untextured | `$0.40` |
| From a description, textured | `$0.60` |
| From a description, textured, rigged with an idle animation | `$0.76` |

A built model ([`build_3d`](/docs/capabilities/3d), [`POST /v1/computers/{id}/build-3d`](/docs/api/computers#build-a-3d-model)) has no price of its own: it runs on the agent's computer and is billed as that computer's running seconds, on the `computer` component. On an agent's computer ($0.0666 an hour) a CAD part with three 768 px previews takes about a minute and a half, about `$0.002\`; the first call also installs the toolchain, about 20 seconds more.

### Browser — per session minute and per hosted action, `browser` component

| Line | Price |
| - | - |
| Session minutes, `opened_at` → `closed_at`, rounded up, **minimum one minute** | `$0.001667` per minute (`$0.10` per hour) |
| One model-driven action — `act`, `extract` with an instruction, `observe` | `$0.010` |

The minutes are one debit when the session closes; there is no up-front hold, because a session's cost is knowable only at close. A session is capped at **360 minutes** (`timeout_minutes`); one that hits its timeout bills up to it and no further. The deterministic actions (`goto`, `click`, `type`, `screenshot`, `links`, …) cost nothing beyond the minutes they run in. The whole model is on [Limits & billing](/docs/computer/limits-and-billing#the-browser).

### Voice calls — per started minute, `voice` component

| What | Price |
| - | - |
| Call minutes, connect → hang-up, rounded up, **minimum one minute** | `$0.08` per minute |

The minutes are one debit when the call ends. Starting a call needs a balance of at least one minute (otherwise `402 insufficient_credits`), a call is capped at **10 minutes** (`$0.80`), and a call whose balance runs out mid-way is told so and hung up. What the agent says is billed as model inference, exactly as in a typed chat.

### Mobile sandbox — per phone-minute, `mobile` component

| Line | Price |
| - | - |
| Android phone minutes, `created_at` → `terminated_at`, rounded up, **minimum one minute** | `$0.050000` per minute (`$3.00` per hour) |
| iPhone minutes, the same way | `$0.080000` per minute (`$4.80` per hour) |

Each rate is the phone plus its network: every phone's traffic exits through a residential IP in its jurisdiction, and `$0.02` of each minute is that network. The minutes are one debit when the device ends — on delete, on its idle timer, at its maximum duration, or when the platform stops it because the balance or plan no longer covers it (`termination_reason: "unfunded"`). There is no up-front hold. Looks, taps, app installs and every other action cost nothing beyond the minutes they run in, and a device that fails to provision bills nothing (one still not ready 10 minutes after its create is ended `failed`). Creating one needs a balance that covers 10 minutes of every live phone and the new one at their rates (`$0.50` for one Android phone, `$0.80` for one iPhone). The whole model is on [Limits & billing](/docs/computer/limits-and-billing#mobile-devices).

### Storage — per bucket-day, `storage` component

Storage on a fullstack app is metered per bucket per UTC day it exists, on its own `storage` line — and **no rate is published for it today, so no line is booked**. The tier exists on the [ledger](/docs/api/credits) so a rate can be set without a schema change; until one is, buckets and objects carry no charge beyond the computer time an agent spends using them.

### The model proxy

[`POST /v1/proxy/anthropic/v1/messages`](/docs/api/proxy) is priced exactly like a session's model call — same catalogue, same per-window tariff, same five tiers, same balance. The proxy adds no charge of its own.

## The completion window is the biggest lever

The same model at a different [window](/docs/concepts/completion-window) is a different price. The window is a single field with three wire values — `immediate`, `priority`, and `loose`.

![One model, three completion window lanes — immediate, priority, loose — with latency increasing and tariff decreasing, chosen per request](https://mintcdn.com/vetta/rjfQyQrWaQ5bFTTq/images/completion-window.svg?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=rjfQyQrWaQ5bFTTq\&q=85\&s=b5a7b5f5210feebb2312ab5d20678c29)

| Window | Latency | Relative model tariff |
| - | - | - |
| `immediate` | Answers now | Highest |
| `priority` | Answers soon | Lower |
| `loose` | Answers eventually | Lowest |

You choose the window **per request** — pay the interactive tariff only when a person is waiting; overnight work runs on `loose` for materially less.

On `immediate`, the [router](/docs/concepts/model-router) picks the fastest provider hosting the model rather than the cheapest, because that window exists for the case where a person is waiting. The same model can therefore cost a little more on one call than another — you are billed from what the call actually cost, and the ledger records which provider served it.

## Budgets keep it predictable

Every [agent has a budget](/docs/concepts/budgets): set `cap_micro_usd`, `max_task_micro_usd`, and a `period`. Model calls are quoted before they run, so one that would breach those ceilings is refused rather than discovered on an invoice. Media renders, compute and the web tools are metered from what they actually used and booked afterwards, so a period's spend can finish past its cap — and, where a funded organization exhausts its balance mid-turn, the balance itself can go negative. It is on the ledger either way, never silent.

## Measured, not modelled

All figures are corrected against vendor invoice brackets — list-price rate cards over-state real cost by 1.017x–4.176x. Methodology in [Benchmarks](https://usenaive.ai/blogs/introducing-naive-managed-agents).

> [card] [See the numbers](https://usenaive.ai/blogs/introducing-naive-managed-agents)
>
> Cost per completed task across 15 measured cells.


# Quickstart
Source: https://usenaive.ai/docs/quickstart

Create an agent, give it work, watch it, and read the meter.

Zero to a running agent in five steps. Every command on this page is tested verbatim against a live deploy.

**1. Install the CLI**

```bash theme={"system"}
npm i -g @usenaive-sdk/cli
naive --version
```

> [!NOTE]
>
> Upgrading from `@usenaive-sdk/vetta-cli`? Run `npm rm -g @usenaive-sdk/vetta-cli` first, because both
> packages install the same commands. Your saved login carries over.

Prefer not to install it globally? Every command below also works as
`npx @usenaive-sdk/cli …`.

The snippets below use `jq` to capture ids from JSON output (`… | jq -r .id`) — install it,
or copy the `agt_...` / `ses_...` ids from the output by hand.

Working with a coding agent? Point it at the onboarding manifest —
[https://usenaive.ai/skill.md](https://usenaive.ai/skill.md) — and it will walk your operator
through everything on this page. Every command below is also a REST call against
[the API](/docs/api/overview), so `curl` works before the CLI does.

**2. Authenticate**

The CLI stores a **profile** — a credential plus base URL — and never prints it back.

```bash theme={"system"}
read -rs KEY && printf '%s\n' "$KEY" | naive login   # an API key, piped so it stays out of shell history
naive login --email you@example.com --password '…'   # a person: signs in, stores a session token
```

Confirm which organization you are pointed at before you spend anything:

```bash theme={"system"}
naive whoami
```

> [!NOTE]
>
> `NAIVE_API_KEY` and `--api-base-url` override the stored profile for a single command, so
> scripts and CI never need a config file at all.

**3. Start the plan**

A new organization needs a plan before anything outside billing answers. Standard is $20 a
        month with $20 of credit included, and starts with a 7-day free trial (card required); Pro is
$200 a month with $200 included. `subscribe` prints a hosted checkout link.

```bash theme={"system"}
naive plan subscribe                # Standard; add --plan pro for Pro
naive plan show                     # status: active once the checkout completes
```

See [Pricing](/docs/platform/pricing#plans).

**4. Add credits**

Billing is real US dollars, prepaid; the plan's included credit lands here too and rolls over.
`topup` prints a hosted checkout link — nothing is credited until the payment settles.

```bash theme={"system"}
naive credits topup --usd 50        # prints a hosted checkout link
naive credits show
```

Your organization is the billing entity; every agent draws from the same balance. See
[Billing](/docs/platform/billing).

**5. Create an agent**

An agent bundles a model, a system prompt, a completion window, and a budget — the budget is
required, so every agent has a spend cap from birth.

```bash theme={"system"}
AGENT=$(naive agent create \
  --name nightly-triage \
  --model z-ai/glm-5.3-flash \
  --budget-usd 50 --max-task-usd 5 --budget-period month \
  --window immediate \
  --system "You are a concise triage agent. You have a Linux sandbox. Do the work, then answer in one short paragraph." \
  | jq -r .id)

echo "$AGENT"     # agt_...
```

Later commands take the **id**, not the name. `naive models list` prints the model ids and the
completion windows each supports.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **You do not attach a computer to an agent.** Each agent gets its own computer the first time
> one of its sessions' tools needs it, and every session of the agent works on it and sees the
> same files — a text-only agent never gets one and pays nothing for it.

**6. Run it and stream the output**

A session is one directly-controlled run: create it with its first message, then stream events.

```bash theme={"system"}
SID=$(naive session create \
  --agent "$AGENT" \
  --message "Create notes.md in your home directory containing 'hello from naive', read it back, and tell me what it says." \
  | jq -r .id)

naive session stream --session "$SID"
```

The stream is the whole truth of the run — every model call with its quote, every tool call,
the reply, the usage line:

```json theme={"system"}
{"seq":4,"type":"tool.started","data":{"name":"write","args":{"path":"~/notes.md","content":"hello from naive"}}}
{"seq":5,"type":"tool.completed","data":{"name":"write","output":"Successfully wrote 16 bytes","is_error":false}}
{"seq":13,"type":"message.completed","data":{"role":"assistant","content":"Done — notes.md contains exactly: hello from naive."}}
{"seq":14,"type":"session.usage","data":{"consumed_micro_usd":2023,"active_seconds":7,"tool_calls":2}}
{"seq":15,"type":"session.idle","data":{"stop_reason":"end_turn"}}
```

Follow up with `naive session send --session "$SID" --text "…"`; resume a dropped stream with
`--after-seq`.

**7. Read the meter**

Every dollar is metered per component, per agent, and per session.

```bash theme={"system"}
naive agent spend "$AGENT" --by component
naive session usage --session "$SID"
```

Files the agent published during the run are listed with
`naive file list --scope session --session "$SID"`.

## Create an API key for programmatic access

Code authenticates with a **scoped API key** — the secret is returned once and never again:

```bash theme={"system"}
naive keys create --name quickstart --scopes agents:read,agents:write,sessions:read,sessions:write
export NAIVE_API_KEY="sk_...the secret shown once..."
```

From TypeScript, use the key with the [TypeScript SDK](/docs/sdk/typescript). It is ESM-only: set
`"type": "module"` in `package.json` (or use `.mts` / `.mjs` files), or load it with
`await import("@usenaive-sdk/managed-agents")` inside an async function in a CommonJS project (if `tsc`
builds it, set `"module"` to `"node16"` or `"nodenext"`, or tsc turns the import into `require()`).

## Driving a sandbox directly

A computer is a disposable Linux sandbox you can drive yourself, independently of any agent.
Pause it and it bills nothing. Sessions work on their agent's own computer — a computer you create
here is never handed to one. See the [Computer reference](/docs/computer/index).

```bash theme={"system"}
naive computer create --name box --vcpu 2 --memory-mb 4096 --disk-gb 20
naive computer exec cmp_... --command 'ls -a ~'
naive computer pause cmp_...
```

## The same arc over HTTP

The CLI is a thin client over the REST API; the whole arc above is a few requests.

```bash theme={"system"}
export NAIVE_API_KEY="sk_..."
export BASE="https://api.vetta.sh"   

AGENT=$(curl -sS "$BASE/v1/agents" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $NAIVE_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "name": "nightly-triage",
    "model": "z-ai/glm-5.3-flash",
    "window": "immediate",
    "system": "You are a concise triage agent.",
    "budget": { "cap_micro_usd": 50000000, "max_task_micro_usd": 5000000, "period": "month" }
  }' | jq -r .id)

SESSION=$(curl -sS "$BASE/v1/sessions" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $NAIVE_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "{\"agent_id\": \"$AGENT\", \"message\": \"Summarize what you can see in your sandbox.\"}" \
  | jq -r .id)

curl -sN "$BASE/v1/sessions/$SESSION/stream" -H "Authorization: Bearer $NAIVE_API_KEY"
```

See the [API overview](/docs/api/overview) for auth, pagination, idempotency and the shared error envelope.

> [card] [Next: how Naive Managed Agents works](/docs/how-managed-agents-is-built)
>
> Harness, runtime, tools — the three layers that make a finished task cheap.


# ads
Source: https://usenaive.ai/docs/sdk/ads

Paused-first paid campaign operations — client.ads.

The SDK exposes the [paid advertising primitive](/docs/api/ads) through `client.ads`. A connected Google
Ads account pays media charges directly; Naive credits are not a media wallet. It is enabled per
organization in early access; elsewhere every call but `pause` throws `feature_not_configured`.

## createSearchCampaign

```ts theme={"system"}
const campaign = await client.ads.createSearchCampaign({
  provider: "google",
  connection_id: connectionId,
  customer_id: "1234567890",
  name: "Founder Frame launch",
  final_url: "https://founderframehq.com/",
  budget_micro_usd: 50_000_000,
  cpc_ceiling_micro_usd: 4_000_000,
  start_date: "2026-10-01",
  end_date: "2026-10-08",
  keywords: ["b2b content agency"],
  headlines: ["Content That Earns Attention", "Founder Frame", "B2B Content Systems"],
  descriptions: ["Turn expert insight into demand.", "Build a repeatable content engine."],
})
// campaign.status === "paused"
```

This call is live-key-only and idempotent. It creates enabled children behind one paused campaign,
so the campaign is complete but cannot spend before activation.

## listCampaigns and insights

```ts theme={"system"}
const account = { connection_id: connectionId, customer_id: "1234567890" }
const campaigns = await client.ads.listCampaigns(account)
const results = await client.ads.insights(campaign.id, account)
```

Both are live provider reads. `results.spend_micro_usd` is external media spend reported by the ad
account.

Every call but `createSearchCampaign` takes the connected ad account as `{ connection_id,
customer_id }`; there is no list across accounts. Leaving it out, or either field, rejects with an
`ApiError` `validation_failed` (status 400) whose `param` names the missing field, before anything
is sent.

## activate and pause

```ts theme={"system"}
await client.ads.activate(campaign.id, {
  ...account,
  acknowledge_external_spend: true,
})

await client.ads.pause(campaign.id, account)
```

Activation can incur external charges and makes the acknowledgement part of the TypeScript type.
It is limited to campaigns Naive created for the same connected account, and it rechecks the finite
provider budget, configured maximum, and end date before enabling. Pause remains available
independently.


# agents
Source: https://usenaive.ai/docs/sdk/agents

Create, version, and retire agents — client.agents, one method per route.

The agent is the durable, versioned configuration a [session](/docs/sdk/sessions) runs. Ten methods, one per route; objects parse with the core `AgentSchema`. API detail: [Agents](/docs/api/agents).

## create

```ts theme={"system"}
client.agents.create(body: AgentCreate): Promise<Agent>
```

`POST /v1/agents`. `AgentCreate` requires `name` (1–100 characters), `model` (an id `client.models.list()` publishes, or `vetta/auto`) and `budget` (`max_task_micro_usd` at most `cap_micro_usd`); everything else on the agent config (`system`, `window`, `harness`, …) is optional. `harness` selects the agent loop and defaults to `pi`; [`client.harnesses.list()`](/docs/sdk/harnesses) publishes the set you can choose from.

```ts theme={"system"}
const budget = { cap_micro_usd: 50_000_000, max_task_micro_usd: 5_000_000, period: "month" } as const; // $50 / $5
const agent = await client.agents.create({ name: "support", model: "...", budget });
// `handoffs` (type `Handoffs`, exported): who it may send work to with `send_to_agent` —
// `true` (any agent of the organization, the default), `false`, "team" (its roster), or agent names.
const closed = await client.agents.create({ name: "auditor", model: "...", budget, handoffs: false });
// `model_selection` (type `ModelSelectionPolicy`): pick one of these ids per turn; `model` is the default.
const picker = await client.agents.create({
  name: "triage",
  model: "a/one",
  budget,
  model_selection: { options: { "a/one": "routine chat", "b/two": "hard reasoning" }, min_confidence: 0.5 },
});
```

## list

```ts theme={"system"}
client.agents.list(query?: ListQuery): Promise<Page<Agent>>
```

`GET /v1/agents`, cursor-paginated. See [Pagination](/docs/sdk/pagination).

## get

```ts theme={"system"}
client.agents.get(id: string): Promise<Agent>
```

`GET /v1/agents/{id}`.

## update

```ts theme={"system"}
client.agents.update(id: string, body: AgentPatch): Promise<Agent>
```

`PATCH /v1/agents/{id}`. Every config field is optional; a successful patch **mints a new version** rather than editing the current one. Pass `expected_version` for optimistic concurrency — a mismatch is a `409 conflict`.

## listVersions

```ts theme={"system"}
client.agents.listVersions(id: string): Promise<Page<AgentVersion>>
```

`GET /v1/agents/{id}/versions`. History is immutable and never rewritten.

## getVersion

```ts theme={"system"}
client.agents.getVersion(id: string, version: number): Promise<AgentVersion>
```

`GET /v1/agents/{id}/versions/{version}`.

## rollback

```ts theme={"system"}
client.agents.rollback(id: string, body: { to_version: number; expected_version?: number }): Promise<Agent>
```

`POST /v1/agents/{id}/rollback`. Mints a **new** version cloning `to_version` — a rollback is itself a versioned change, so history stays linear and auditable.

## spend

```ts theme={"system"}
client.agents.spend(id: string, query?: { by?: "component" }): Promise<AgentSpend>
```

`GET /v1/agents/{id}/spend` — metered spend for the agent's current budget period, integer micro-USD:

```json theme={"system"}
{ "agent_id": "agt_01H...", "period": "month", "period_start": "2026-08-01T00:00:00Z", "spent_micro_usd": 1250000 }
```

`by: "component"` adds a `by_component` breakdown — `model` (the five token tiers summed), `computer`, `search`, `media`, and `other` for anything a debit did not itemise. A component with no spend is absent, and the breakdown always sums to `spent_micro_usd`. Absent unless asked for.

Computer time is billed to the agent and to no session, so `spent_micro_usd` is more than the agent's sessions' `consumed_micro_usd` added up; `computer` is the difference.

## computer

```ts theme={"system"}
client.agents.computer(id: string): Promise<Computer | null>
```

`GET /v1/agents/{id}/computer`. The agent's one [computer](/docs/sdk/computers), which every session of the agent works on, or `null` before any session has needed one. The machine under it can change while its files are kept, so read this rather than caching a `cmp_` id. See [An agent's computer](/docs/api/computers#an-agents-computer).

## delete

```ts theme={"system"}
client.agents.delete(id: string): Promise<Deleted & { removed_from: { id: string; name: string; version: number }[] }>
```

`DELETE /v1/agents/{id}`. Answers the standard `{ id, object, deleted: true }` acknowledgement, plus `removed_from`: every coordinator whose team roster named this agent and now has a new version without it. Empty when the agent was on no roster.

> [!WARNING]
>
> Deleting an agent also deletes every [deployment](/docs/sdk/deployments) that runs it, so its schedules stop firing. Nothing asks first; list them with `client.deployments.list()` before you delete.


# apps
Source: https://usenaive.ai/docs/sdk/apps

Hosted web applications — client.apps.

An app is **org-level**: it belongs to the organization, not to an agent, and outlives any session. Thirty-five methods: twenty on an app itself, plus `installs.apply` / `installs.list` / `installs.update` / `installs.context` / `installs.remove` / `installs.preview` for the declaration a project is applied from and what its crew knows, `artifacts.list` for the catalog it is applied out of, `companyTemplates.draft` / `companyTemplates.create` / `companyTemplates.list` for a company saved as a private template, `listings.list` / `listings.checks` for the company's marketplace listings and what a new one would send, `profile.get` / `profile.update` for the public profile its listings credit, and `earnings.setUpPayouts` for where its earnings are paid. API detail: [Apps](/docs/api/apps).

## create

```ts theme={"system"}
client.apps.create(body: AppCreate): Promise<App>
```

`POST /v1/apps`. `AppCreate` is `{ name, description?, type?, mcp? }` — `type` is `"frontend_only"` (default) or `"fullstack"`; `mcp` is the path of the MCP endpoint a `fullstack` app serves (`"/mcp"`), refused on `frontend_only`. Idempotent on the name.

## list

```ts theme={"system"}
client.apps.list(query?: ListQuery): Promise<Page<App>>
```

`GET /v1/apps`, cursor-paginated.

## get

```ts theme={"system"}
client.apps.get(id: string): Promise<App>
```

`GET /v1/apps/{id}`. A `fullstack` app's backend advances on read — poll here until `status` is terminal.

## update

```ts theme={"system"}
client.apps.update(id: string, body: AppPatch): Promise<App>
```

`PATCH /v1/apps/{id}`. `AppPatch` is `{ description?: string | null, mcp?: string | null }`. Setting `mcp` mints the app's `VETTA_MCP_TOKEN` secret and connects every agent that can access the app to its tools as `<app>.<tool>`; `null` removes both. See [Tools from your apps](/docs/capabilities/tools#tools-from-your-apps).

## delete

```ts theme={"system"}
client.apps.delete(id: string): Promise<Deleted>
```

`DELETE /v1/apps/{id}`. Tears down the hosting project and, for `fullstack`, the app database. Irreversible.

## deploy

```ts theme={"system"}
client.apps.deploy(id: string, files: Record<string, string>, content_hash?: string): Promise<AppDeployment>
```

`POST /v1/apps/{id}/deployments`. `files` maps paths to base64 contents; the build runs asynchronously. `content_hash` is an opaque digest of `files` you compute (up to 128 characters). The platform stores it as sent, never checks it, and echoes it on every deployment read, so you can compare it against the newest deployment and skip uploading an unchanged site.

## redeploy

```ts theme={"system"}
client.apps.redeploy(id: string, fromDeployment: string): Promise<AppDeployment>
```

`POST /v1/apps/{id}/deployments` with `{ from_deployment }`. Ships one of the app's earlier deployments again, as a new deployment, from the files the platform kept — nothing is uploaded, so a site of any deployable size comes back. Poll [`deployments`](#deployments) as for `deploy`.

## deploymentFiles

```ts theme={"system"}
client.apps.deploymentFiles(id: string, deploymentId: string): Promise<AppDeploymentFiles>
```

`GET /v1/apps/{id}/deployments/{deployment_id}/files`. The file map a deployment shipped: `{ object: "app_deployment_files", deployment_id, files }`, path → base64. `not_found` for a build made before files were kept.

## deployments

```ts theme={"system"}
client.apps.deployments(id: string, query?: { limit?: number }): Promise<Page<AppDeployment>>
```

`GET /v1/apps/{id}/deployments`. Non-terminal builds advance on read.

## setSecret

```ts theme={"system"}
client.apps.setSecret(id: string, body: { name: string; value: string }): Promise<AppSecret>
```

`POST /v1/apps/{id}/secrets`. Write-only: the value never comes back on any read. Overwrites an existing name. The names the platform manages itself — a `fullstack` app's `DATABASE_*` variables and `VETTA_MCP_TOKEN` (set through [`update`](#update)'s `mcp`) — are refused `forbidden`.

## secrets

```ts theme={"system"}
client.apps.secrets(id: string): Promise<{ object: "list"; data: AppSecret[] }>
```

`GET /v1/apps/{id}/secrets` — names and timestamps only, never values.

## deleteSecret

```ts theme={"system"}
client.apps.deleteSecret(id: string, name: string): Promise<{ object: "app_secret"; name: string; deleted: boolean }>
```

`DELETE /v1/apps/{id}/secrets/{name}`. A platform-managed name (see [`setSecret`](#setsecret)) is refused `forbidden`.

## connectDomain

```ts theme={"system"}
client.apps.connectDomain(id: string, domainId: string): Promise<AppDomain>
```

`POST /v1/apps/{id}/domains`. The domain must already exist at [`client.domains`](/docs/sdk/domains); connecting is pointing, never registering.

## domains

```ts theme={"system"}
client.apps.domains(id: string): Promise<{ object: "list"; data: AppDomain[] }>
```

`GET /v1/apps/{id}/domains`.

## disconnectDomain

```ts theme={"system"}
client.apps.disconnectDomain(id: string, domain: string): Promise<{ object: "app_domain"; domain: string; deleted: boolean }>
```

`DELETE /v1/apps/{id}/domains/{domain}` — by domain name.

## entry

```ts theme={"system"}
client.apps.entry(id: string): Promise<{ object: "app_entry"; url: string; ticket: string }>
```

`POST /v1/apps/{id}/entry`. A one-click way into an app whose operator gate the platform generated. Answers a `ticket` valid for two minutes, never the app's token: POST it to `url` as a form field from the operator's browser, and never put it in a query string.

## permissions

```ts theme={"system"}
client.apps.permissions(id: string): Promise<{ object: "app_permissions"; app_id: string; scopes: string[] }>
```

`GET /v1/apps/{id}/permissions`. What the app's own key may do: its scopes, never the key.

## access

```ts theme={"system"}
client.apps.access(id: string): Promise<{ object: "app_access"; url: string | null; password: string | null }>
```

`GET /v1/apps/{id}/access`. How a person gets into the app without the Studio: its URL and its generated `DASHBOARD_PASSWORD` — `null` until one is provisioned. An audited reveal; hand the value to a person, never put it in a URL or a log.

## rotateAccess

```ts theme={"system"}
client.apps.rotateAccess(id: string): Promise<{ object: "app_access"; url: string | null; password: string | null }>
```

`POST /v1/apps/{id}/access`. Regenerates the password **and** the `DASHBOARD_TOKEN`, and answers the new password. Rotating is revoking: every browser already signed in is signed out.

## query

```ts theme={"system"}
client.apps.query(id: string, query: string): Promise<{ object: "app_db_result"; rows: unknown[]; row_count: number }>
```

`POST /v1/apps/{id}/db/query`. `fullstack` apps only; a `frontend_only` app answers `feature_not_configured`. The database as a whole — tables, a REST facade over them, migrations, and this same query without naming the app — is [`client.database`](/docs/sdk/database).

## installs.apply

```ts theme={"system"}
client.apps.installs.apply(body: InstallApply): Promise<BlueprintInstall>
```

`POST /v1/blueprints/installs`. Records one applied declaration for a project — with what, by whom, and against which revision — and, when you name a published pair instead of sending one, performs the apply too.

Sending a `declaration` records only, and that is the right shape for this client: you reconciled it yourself, which is the upsert-by-name every other method here performs, so `report` comes back `null`. Omitting the declaration and naming a published `blueprint` and `template` asks the server to reconcile the catalog's bytes for you, as you, and `report` is what that run did — one line per resource, refusals included.

`expected_revision` is [`expected_version`](/docs/api/agents) copied: omit it for a deliberate unconditional apply, or send the revision you believe you are moving from and a mismatch is refused `revision_conflict`, whose message names the paths at which the stored declaration and yours disagree. Send `0` to create: a project that already exists is refused rather than re-applied.

`selection: { agents: string[]; apps: string[] }` names which of the template's crew this apply provisions; omit it and the whole crew is. A deselected agent is not created, its schedules are not armed and its intake does not open; one that already exists is left running, and the report names it under `deselected` — apart from `skipped`, because a choice is not a failure. A selection that leaves out a `required` agent or app is refused `validation_failed`, naming every missing one. The install stores the `selection` it was applied with (`null` for everything, and for every install written before the field existed). See [Templates](/docs/concepts/templates).

## installs.list

```ts theme={"system"}
client.apps.installs.list(query?: { project?: string; limit?: number; after?: string }): Promise<Page<BlueprintInstall>>
```

`GET /v1/blueprints/installs`. Every install in the organization, most recently applied first; `project` narrows it to one project's.

## installs.update

```ts theme={"system"}
client.apps.installs.update(id: string, body: { answers: Record<string, unknown> }): Promise<BlueprintInstall>
```

`PATCH /v1/blueprints/installs/{id}`. Rewrites the setup answers of an applied install — the whole map, not a merge, so send every answer you mean to keep. Each key must be a question the install's artifact declares, and each value a string or a list of strings; anything else is refused `validation_failed`. The install's `context_updated_at` moves and its `revision` does not: an answer edit is not an apply, re-provisions nothing and briefs no agent again. The crew reads the new answer through [`installs.context`](#installscontext) the next time it looks.

## installs.context

```ts theme={"system"}
client.apps.installs.context(id: string): Promise<ProjectContext>
```

`GET /v1/blueprints/installs/{id}/context`. What the crew of this install knows about the business: `{ object: "project_context", project, blueprint, template, artifact_version, answers: { key, label, value }[], apps: { name, url }[], agents: { name, role }[], updated_at }`, derived from the install and its report — the answers as the artifact's questions label them, the apps with the URL each is served at, the agents with the role each was declared with. It is the same object a template agent reads through its built-in `project_context` tool.

## installs.remove

```ts theme={"system"}
client.apps.installs.remove(id: string): Promise<{ id: string; object: string; deleted: boolean }>
```

`DELETE /v1/blueprints/installs/{id}`. Takes a template out of the company: its agents are fired (their timers stop, their open cards lose their name), its unfinished board tasks and its mini apps go, and the install is deleted. Its apps, personas, skills, files and chats stay. Nothing is refunded or charged. Only the owner's own sign-in may call it; an API key is refused `forbidden`. A second call is `not_found`.

## installs.preview

```ts theme={"system"}
client.apps.installs.preview(query: { blueprint: string; template: string; project: string }): Promise<InstallPreview>
```

`GET /v1/blueprints/preview`. What applying a published pair as a new project would call its agents, apps and personas here: `{ object: "install_preview", project, blueprint, template, artifact_version, name_prefix, agents, apps, identities }`. `name_prefix` is `"<project>-"` when any declared name is already taken in the organization, and every name then carries it. Writes nothing.

## artifacts.list

```ts theme={"system"}
client.apps.artifacts.list(query?: {
  blueprint?: string; template?: string; limit?: number; after?: string;
}): Promise<Page<BlueprintArtifact> & { skipped: number }>
```

`GET /v1/blueprints/artifacts`. The published catalog, newest release first — every blueprint × template that can be run, carrying the setup questions to ask first, the crew and the apps it provisions, and the timers it runs.

The catalog belongs to no organization: it is the same list for everybody, and nothing a customer writes reaches it. Applying one of these rows sends its `blueprint` and `template` in place of a `declaration`, which the catalog holds server-side.

## companyTemplates.draft

```ts theme={"system"}
client.apps.companyTemplates.draft(body?: { project?: string }): Promise<CompanyTemplateDraft>
```

`POST /v1/company_templates/draft`. "Duplicate this company": exports the crew and rewrites its company specifics into a draft declaration. A metered model call.

## companyTemplates.create

```ts theme={"system"}
client.apps.companyTemplates.create(body: { name: string; project?: string; declaration: CompanyTemplateDraft["declaration"] }): Promise<BlueprintArtifact>
```

`POST /v1/company_templates`. Saves a draft a person approved as a **private** template of this organization. Install it with `installs.apply({ blueprint, template, project, expected_revision: 0 })`; no other organization can.

## companyTemplates.list

```ts theme={"system"}
client.apps.companyTemplates.list(query?: { template?: string; limit?: number; after?: string }): Promise<Page<BlueprintArtifact> & { skipped: number }>
```

`GET /v1/company_templates`. This organization's private templates, as catalog rows.

## listings.checks

```ts theme={"system"}
client.apps.listings.checks(query?: { project?: string }): Promise<ListingChecks>
```

`GET /v1/listings/checks`. What listing the company in the marketplace would send — the changes made, anything refused, and every word that would be listed. Read only: a listing is posted from chat, not from the SDK.

## listings.list

```ts theme={"system"}
client.apps.listings.list(): Promise<OwnListings>
```

`GET /v1/listings`. The company's own marketplace listings, newest first, each with its review `status` and whether it was `taken_down`. `balance_micro_usd` is what they earned and not yet paid out, and `ready_micro_usd` the part a payout would send now; both are `null` for a key without `billing:read`.

## profile.get

```ts theme={"system"}
client.apps.profile.get(): Promise<CreatorProfile>
```

`GET /v1/listings/profile`. The company's public profile, which its listed templates credit: `handle`, `name`, `description`, `avatar_url` and `verified`.

## profile.update

```ts theme={"system"}
client.apps.profile.update(body: {
  name?: string;
  description?: string;
  avatar?: { content_type: "image/png" | "image/jpeg" | "image/webp"; data: string } | null;
}): Promise<CreatorProfile>
```

`PATCH /v1/listings/profile`. `name` is 1–60 characters and `description` at most 280. `avatar` is a base64 picture of at most 512 KiB, and `null` removes it. Only a signed-in owner or admin may update the profile; anyone else, an API key included, is `forbidden`.

## earnings.setUpPayouts

```ts theme={"system"}
client.apps.earnings.setUpPayouts(body?: { country?: string }): Promise<{ object: "earnings_payout_account"; ready: boolean; onboarding_url: string | null }>
```

`POST /v1/earnings/payouts/account`. Where the company's marketplace earnings are paid. The owner, signed in, opens `onboarding_url` until `ready` is `true`.


# auditLogs
Source: https://usenaive.ai/docs/sdk/audit-logs

The control-plane trail — client.auditLogs.

One method. The trail is read-only by construction: it only grows. API detail: [Audit logs](/docs/api/audit-logs).

## list

```ts theme={"system"}
client.auditLogs.list(query?: AuditFilter): Promise<Page<AuditEntry> & { skipped: number }>
```

`GET /v1/audit_logs`. `AuditFilter` extends the [page query](/docs/sdk/pagination) with:

**actor** `string`

A principal id — a member `usr_…` or a key `key_…`.

**resource** `string`

A resource id, e.g. one `agt_…`.

**action** `string`

An action name, e.g. `member.role_changed`.

**request\_id** `string`

Only the entries one request wrote, by its `request_id`: the `x-request-id` header on its response, which a failed call also reports as [`ApiError.requestId`](/docs/sdk/errors).

**from** `string`

Start of the time range (ISO 8601).

**to** `string`

End of the time range.

```ts theme={"system"}
const trail = await client.auditLogs.list({ resource: agent.id, limit: 50 });
```


# auth
Source: https://usenaive.ai/docs/sdk/auth

Who am I, person sign-in, registration, and recovery — client.auth.

Eight methods. Everything else in the client authenticates with the `apiKey` the client was constructed with; this namespace is how a **person** gets a credential in the first place. API detail: [Authentication](/docs/api/authentication).

## me

```ts theme={"system"}
client.auth.me(): Promise<Identity>
```

`GET /v1/me` — who this credential is: principal, organization, scopes, and (for a person) email and role. The first call any client makes, and the reason none of them needs an `org_` id as input.

## session

```ts theme={"system"}
client.auth.session(body: { email?: string; password?: string; organization_id?: string }): Promise<AuthSession>
```

`POST /v1/auth/session`. Two uses of one route:

* **Sign in** with `email` + `password` — answers a short-lived `vt_` bearer `token`, its `expires_at`, and the person's `organizations`.
* **Re-scope**: present an existing `vt_` token (as the client's `apiKey`) with an `organization_id` to switch organizations. An org you are not a member of is a `404 not_found`, the same answer as one that does not exist.

The `token` is a bearer credential — never put it in a browser.

## register

```ts theme={"system"}
client.auth.register(body: { email: string; password: string }): Promise<{ object: "auth_user"; email: string; confirmation_required: boolean; hint?: string }>
```

`POST /v1/auth/users`. `confirmation_required: true` means the address must be confirmed by mail before sign-in succeeds — the response never pretends the person is signed in.
